articles.title: Most Reliable SUVs With Good Gas Mileage: The Brand That Beat Toyota Also Does 30 MPG
articles.summary: Toyota finished eighth in J.D. Power's 2026 dependability study. The mass-market winner gets 30 mpg.
articles.body:
Autoblog and Yahoo may earn commission from links in this article.

The mpg number on a window sticker comes out of a lab test, run on the car sitting in the showroom this afternoon. Dependability data works the other way round. It comes from asking owners who bought three years ago how the thing has held up since. Shopping for a reliable SUV with good gas mileage means using both at once, and the list that holds up under both is shorter than you would expect.

The industry average in this year's dependability study reached 204 problems per 100 vehicles. Fewer problems is the better score, and this year's average was the worst since the study was rebuilt in 2022. The brand that finished first among mass-market makers was not Toyota, Honda, or Subaru. It was Buick, at 160, for the second year running. Toyota came eighth at 185. Every score below comes from that 2026 study, which surveyed 33,268 owners of 2023 model-year cars, and every mpg figure comes from fueleconomy.gov.

Honda came in at 211 PP100, worse than the 204 industry average , which keeps the gas CR-V and its 30 combined off this list. Hyundai cleared that average comfortably, at 198, and its case for inclusion gets its own section below.

It's the highest-mpg SUV you can buy without an electric motor, rated 31 city and 33 highway with front-wheel drive, and nothing else in the class matches the combined number.

Other lists still put the Nissan Kicks Play first at 33 combined, but Nissan stopped building it after 2025 and there is no 2026 version to buy.

Toyota's 185 PP100 is eighth overall and well clear of the industry average. The catch is size. This is the smallest, cheapest SUV Toyota sells here, and adding all-wheel drive costs two mpg, dropping the gas car to 30 combined.

View the 3 images of this gallery on the original article

Twenty-nine city, 36 highway, 32 combined with front-wheel drive, 31 with all-wheel drive. That highway figure is the best in this group and does more real-world work than a combined number if your week is mostly interstate. The AWD Rock Creek trim drops to 29 combined, a real cost for what is mostly an appearance package.

The smaller Kicks is the other half of Nissan's case here, at 31 combined with front-wheel drive and 30 with all-wheel drive. That is the narrowest all-wheel-drive penalty of any vehicle on this list, one mpg, and it undercuts the Rogue on price.

Nissan finished at 194 PP100, tenth in the ranking. The brand clears the industry average without clearing it by much.

Both crossovers return 31 mpg combined, matching the Volkswagen Taos below and beating every all-wheel-drive-only option on this list. Hyundai's 198 PP100 clears the industry average of 204 comfortably, though neither model has won a dependability award outright.

Worth knowing before you shop it: for 2026 the Seltos is all-wheel drive only. The 2.0-liter returns 27 city, 31 highway, 29 combined, and the 1.6-liter turbo drops to 25 combined. With no front-drive version to buy, it lands below the Taos and the Envista here despite being the newer design.

Kia sits at 193 PP100, ninth overall and a single point ahead of Nissan.

The only vehicle here holding a model-level award rather than a brand average. J.D. Power named it most dependable in its segment , and Subaru placed sixth overall at 181 PP100.

Twenty-six city, 33 highway, 29 combined on the base engine, and 26 combined on the Wilderness. That is level with the Seltos, which is the only other all-wheel-drive vehicle here, and Subaru's 181 PP100 sits twelve points ahead of Kia's. So it does the same mpg as the Seltos, from a brand that scored better, and it has the award the Kia never won.

Volkswagen Taos: 31 MPG Combined, And The Worst Score In The Study

Thirty-one combined puts the Taos level with the Kicks and the Hyundai pair, and ahead of both all-wheel-drive options here. Volkswagen also finished last of every brand measured, at 301 PP100. That is 97 problems per 100 vehicles worse than average and nearly double Buick's score.

It belongs on a list of the best fuel efficient SUVs and nowhere near a list of dependable ones.

Buick Encore GX: 30 MPG Combined, And The Best Score In The Study

Buick's 160 PP100 is the best mass-market result for the second consecutive year. It also finished third among mass-market brands in J.D. Power's initial quality study in June, at 162. The two studies ask different questions and Buick placed in the top three of both.

Buick rates the Encore GX at 30 combined with front-wheel drive, on either the 1.2-liter or the 1.3-liter turbo three, falling to 27 combined with the 1.3 and all-wheel drive. The Envista, front-drive only, is 28 city, 32 highway, 30 combined.

The Envista arrived for 2024, though, so it was not in the 2023 sample the study measured. Buick's 160 was earned by the Encore GX, the Envision, and the Enclave. If you want the Buick whose score is actually built on owners of that car, it is the Encore GX.

The Chevrolet Trax is the same vehicle underneath, same 1.2-liter turbo three, same six-speed automatic, same front-drive-only layout, rated 28 city, 31 highway, 29 combined, and Chevrolet finished third among mass-market brands at 178 PP100. The Trax costs less. The Envista is quieter and better trimmed. Neither offers all-wheel drive, so the Encore GX is the one to order if you need it.

For the highest combined figure, the Corolla Cross. For highway miles, the Rogue. If you need all-wheel drive, the Crosstrek over the Seltos, on the same 29 mpg and a better record.

And if you are willing to look at a badge you had written off, the Encore GX pairs 30 mpg combined with the best mass-market dependability score in the industry, in both of the studies that measure it, and offers all-wheel drive at 27. Nothing else on this list does that. Buick's problem is that nobody expects Buick to be the answer here, which is a marketing failure rather than an engineering one.

None of this is a guarantee. What a three-year-old car did tells you nothing certain about the one on the lot, and every vehicle above is currently being sold in a version that will not turn up in a dependability study until 2028 at the earliest.

articles.title: Birthday cakes, Honda CR-Vs and more: Bedazzling is back, but it has a new name.
articles.summary: Is performative whimsy boring? Some creators think so. Others have fully embraced the playful trend.
articles.body:
Sapphire hearts! Tangerine teardrops! Periwinkle diamonds! Emerald ovals! These were just a handful of the gemstones found on Kylie Jenner's glamorous, now-viral birthday cake. The Khy founder shared a carousel of photos on Instagram from her 29th birthday celebration last month. Among the several snaps from her party was one that particularly captivated the internet: a white-frosted birthday cake dripping in colorful, three-dimensional jewels by cake decorator Cory Pohlman .

Jenner's kitschy confection solidified the summer's most playful pastime: bedazzling. And while the Keeping Up With the Kardashians star by no means started the trend — which some Gen Z and Gen Alpha are referring to as gem-maxxing or whimsymaxxing — her stamp of approval has helped cement its renewed popularity on the internet.

"She gave it cultural permission for it to be cool again," said Ranya Batal , a creative strategist and cultural commentator, of Jenner's influence on bedazzling. "That's social proof. When someone with enough status does something, something that would've looked completely tacky three weeks ago is now the coolest thing in the world."

Gem-maxxing, whimsymaxxing, bedazzling … oh my

Bedazzling (also known as whimsymaxxing and gem-maxxing) is the act of affixing colorful plastic rhinestones and gemstones to any surface of your choosing. The trend leans into a more maximalist aesthetic, one rooted in the celebration of whimsical design sensibilities and unabashedly quirky forms of self-expression.

"To bedazzle is to decorate clothes and accessories with rhinestones, crystals, beads and sequins," according to Google, which said in March that searches for the trend were at "an all-time high," surpassing the previous record set in 2010. Pinterest shared similar findings in April: Searches for "bedazzling ideas" and "bedazzled digital camera" were up 900%, while "bedazzled claw clip" was up 2,000%.

So why is bedazzling having a major moment right now?

"I think part of it is aesthetic fatigue," Batal told Yahoo. "We've spent years in minimalism. Clean girl, quiet luxury, neutrals. Everything has been very polished and restrained, so trends naturally swing in the opposite direction. People are craving personality, color, nostalgia and excess again."

If the bedazzling trend looks familiar, that's because it is. Gen Z and Gen Alpha may be leaning into the trend now, but back in the day, millennials were its target demographic. Bedazzling was a hallmark of the "McBling" aesthetic that reigned supreme during the aughts. According to the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute , a collective that digitally archives past aesthetics, the "McBling" aesthetic represented a "hard shift away from the minimalist futurism of the Y2K era," and embraced "aspirational luxury in all forms."

Think a hot pink Motorola Razr covered in iridescent rhinestones or the iconic, rhinestone-encrusted "Juicy" logo plastered across the back of low-rise velour track pants. Rhinestones were virtually everywhere.

Jenner isn't the only celebrity who's obsessed with bedazzling. Selena Gomez and Benny Blanco have embraced the trend too, opting for colorful gems all over their faces . Swedish pop star Zara Larsson, who's beloved for her joyful, vibrant, tropical-meets-Y2K style, is often decked out in glittery gemstones on and off the stage. Larsson's now-signature makeup is basically a dreamy ode to whimsymaxxing: The "Midnight Sun" singer regularly incorporates rhinestones into her colorful looks.

When it comes to whimsymaxxing, every surface is up for grabs. Case in point? TikTokers who've embraced the maximalist trend have bedazzled just about every object you can think of — from Rhode peptide lip treatments and champagne bottles to Jollibee chicken buckets and Honda CR-Vs ( yes , you read that correctly).

TikTok creator Becca Green documented the process of bedazzling the entire exterior of her Honda CR-V, which she says used 198,000 rhinestones, took 1,200 hours and cost a whopping $10,000.

While some people have gravitated toward bedazzling because of its rhythmic, soothing nature and its relative affordability, others are less keen to follow the trend. Some critics have called whimsymaxxing a wasteful microtrend that serves no purpose other than generating more landfill.

"Performative whimsy done for the sake of social media likes completely derails the concept of being whimsical in the first place," content creator Sarah Magliocco wrote on TikTok. "And every time I've seen this rhinestone sticker trend … all I think about is how the stickers are just extra wasted chunks of discarded plastic being used as props. They are going straight in the bin after these photos are taken."

It's also worth noting that while people may want to express themselves in unique ways, plastering colorful plastic rhinestones on everything could have the opposite effect.

"I'm all for personal expression. Bedazzle your phone, your shoes, your entire refrigerator if it makes you happy," Batal said. "As a millennial, we labeled it bedazzling. But now we have given it a new '-maxxing' name, and suddenly [it's presented] as a cultural movement. There's also something ironic about a trend supposedly centered around individuality becoming incredibly copy-and-paste. Everyone is expressing their individuality in exactly the same way."

The whimsymaxxing movement, Batal argued, is essentially the "completely normal behavior" of "decorating our belongings" repackaged in an enticing, almost status-driven way for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Who knew rhinestones would be so coveted in 2026?

"Gen Z and Gen Alpha have grown up with identity being extremely visual and extremely public. What you wear, what's hanging off your bag, your phone case, your water bottle. All of these little objects become signals about who you are and what cultural group you belong to," she said.

Instagram creator Alyssa Forato argues that the problem isn't the rhinestones, it's the people bedazzling items " because the algorithm said so ."

"Your $5 packet of gems may feel insignificant, but when you put it on a global scale of how many people are now buying into this trend, the waste is excessive," Forato said. "I am not saying be a minimalist, nor am I a minimalist. But before you buy into the next whimsymaxxing trend, ask yourself, 'Is this something you would actually do on an actual regular basis if this wasn't trending?'"

articles.title: These are the happiest states in America. See where your state ranks
articles.summary: A new report from WalletHub has ranked all 50 states for happiness. Here's who came out on top.
articles.body:
Americans may not all agree on what brings happiness, but a new ranking suggests where people are most likely to find it.

WalletHub's annual Happiest States in America report ranked all 50 states using measures tied to emotional and physical well-being, work environment, financial security and community life. Hawaii earned the top spot, followed by New Jersey, Utah, Idaho and Maryland.

The report comes as many Americans continue to navigate economic uncertainty. Citing Gallup data, WalletHub noted that only 44% of Americans say they are "very satisfied" with their lives, suggesting that factors such as health, employment, relationships and financial stability all play a role in overall well-being.

WalletHub based the rankings on 30 metrics spanning health, finances, employment, safety, social connections and other quality-of-life measures.

25 stunning US views every American should see at least once

According to WalletHub, here's where all 50 states ranked when it comes to happiness:

Hawaii topped the rankings thanks to strong scores in health, life satisfaction and financial well-being.

The state had the nation's highest reported life satisfaction and the second-lowest adult depression rate. Around 84% of adults reported being in good or better health, Hawaiians have the longest life expectancy in the country, and nearly 72% of adults said they feel active and productive every day.

Hawaii also performed well economically. Its 2.5% unemployment rate ranked among the nation's lowest, it had the third-highest share of households earning more than $75,000 annually, and residents reported the nation's second-lowest levels of financial anxiety.

New Jersey ranked second, aided by the nation's lowest depression rate and the highest share of residents reporting supportive relationships and love in their lives. The Garden State also had the second-lowest separation and divorce rate and the second-highest share of households earning more than $75,000 annually.

Utah finished third after ranking first for economic security, a measure that considers employment, insurance coverage and financial stability. The state also had the nation's lowest separation and divorce rate, residents worked fewer hours per week than those in any other state, and WalletHub ranked Utah second for weather.

WalletHub based the rankings on factors tied to overall quality of life, including health, finances, employment, safety, social connections and leisure time.

"The happiest states are those that provide above-average quality of life in a wide variety of areas, from strong state economies and great physical and mental healthcare to adequate amounts of leisure time and good weather," WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo said in a statement.

"It's also important to note that while the adage that money can't buy happiness has a lot of truth to it, having enough money to live comfortably is still essential. But anything beyond that won't necessarily enhance happiness as much as having fulfilling hobbies, relationships and opportunities for personal growth."

articles.title: Homem foge da polícia e abandona carro com maconha em Campo Grande | G1
articles.standfirst: Motorista desobedeceu à ordem de parada, fugiu por avenidas da cidade e deixou o veículo às margens da Avenida Marginal Lagoa.
articles.summary: Motorista desobedeceu à ordem de parada, fugiu por avenidas da cidade e deixou o veículo às margens da Avenida Marginal Lagoa.
articles.body:
Um homem está foragido após fugir da polícia e abandonar um carro em uma área de mata, na noite desta quarta-feira (9), na Avenida Marginal Lagoa, em Campo Grande . No veículo, foram apreendidos 921,4 kg de maconha.

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, policiais da Força Tática da 6ª Companhia receberam informações anônimas de que um veículo estaria chegando à cidade com entorpecentes.

Os policiais localizaram o carro e deram ordem de parada ao motorista, que não obedeceu. Ele fugiu pela Avenida Gunter Hans, onde passou por diversos semáforos sem parar.

Na sequência, o motorista seguiu até a Avenida Marginal Lagoa, onde há uma área de mata às margens da pista. Ele abandonou o veículo e continuou a fuga a pé.

Durante a vistoria, os policiais encontraram diversos tabletes de drogas. Ao todo, foram apreendidos 5,2 kg de ice drift, 36,4 kg de skunk e 879,6 kg de maconha prensada.

O veículo e as drogas foram apreendidos e encaminhados à Delegacia Especializada de Repressão ao Narcotráfico (Denar). O motorista ainda não foi localizado.

Droga e veículo foram apreendidos em Campo Grande — Foto: PMMS

articles.title: Donald Trump promete US$ 5 mil a americanos e fim da guerra no Irã | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente americano não detalhou de onde viriam recursos para bancar plano que custaria cerca de US$ 1,3 trilhão (R$ 6,6 trilhões).
articles.summary: Donald Trump propõe pagar US$ 5 mil a americanos e prevê fim da guerra no Irã caso republicanos vençam as eleições nos EUA, apesar de incertezas fiscais.
articles.body:
Trump diz aos apoiadores que o voto deles decidirá se o país "tropeçará" ou 'seguirá em frente'. — Foto: Getty Images

A primeira convenção de meio de mandato do Partido Republicano, nos Estados Unidos, teve todos os elementos de um tradicional encontro de ano eleitoral presidencial: apoiadores com roupas brilhantes, uma sequência ininterrupta de discursos de candidatos e vendedores de artigos de campanha.

Mas, diferentemente de uma convenção comum, nenhum assunto oficial do partido foi tratado em Dallas.

Em vez disso, o evento serviu como um comício para republicanos que buscam aumentar o comparecimento às urnas e evitar perder o controle do Congresso em novembro .

O presidente Donald Trump , cujo domínio sobre o partido continua absoluto, fez um longo discurso principal na quarta-feira, durante a noite de abertura do evento de dois dias.

Entre as falas, Trump prometeu pagar US$ 5 mil (cerca de R$ 25,5 mil) a cada cidadão americano adulto caso os republicanos vençam nas duas Casas do Congresso nas eleições de novembro. Ele não detalhou como o plano funcionaria nem de onde viria o dinheiro.

Também disse que a guerra no Irã vai acabar logo após as eleições de novembro , afirmando que Teerã "não aguenta mais".

Veja abaixo quatro conclusões que podem ser tiradas do evento.4 pontos da fala de Trump em evento eleitoral: 'US$ 5 mil para cada americano' e guerra do Irã vai acabar 'após eleição'

A enorme arena estava cheia de apoiadores fervorosos de Trump usando roupas vermelhas MAGA (sigla para Make America Great Again ) de suas campanhas presidenciais anteriores. Uma década após sua primeira candidatura à Casa Branca, Trump continua amado por sua base e, desde então, dobrou o partido à sua vontade.

A cúpula republicana à moda antiga, ou o que restou dela na era Trump, não estava em lugar algum. A senadora Susan Collins, do Maine, e outros republicanos que disputam eleições acirradas optaram por ficar de fora.

A ausência de republicanos mais moderados era evidente e serviu como lembrete de quanto o partido mudou.

Isso também levantou dúvidas sobre a eficácia de realizar uma convenção de meio de mandato.

O público principal, tanto na arena quanto o que assistia pela televisão, parecia ser formado por pessoas leais a Trump, e não pelos moderados e eleitores indecisos que o Partido Republicano precisa mobilizar em grande número em novembro.

O domínio total de Trump sobre o partido levanta algumas questões pertinentes sobre seu futuro.

Quem o substituirá? E, mais imediatamente, para as eleições de novembro, como o partido se sairá quando o nome dele não estiver na cédula?

Trump ofereceu uma solução simples para a segunda questão na noite de quarta-feira.

Depois de alertar que o presidente em exercício tende a perder as eleições de meio de mandato, ele disse à multidão: "Estou pedindo que vocês finjam que meu nome está na cédula."

A declaração foi um reconhecimento de Trump de que ele continua sendo, no partido, o maior impulsionador para levar eleitores às urnas.

Também evidencia o desafio que os republicanos enfrentam tanto em novembro quanto na próxima eleição presidencial, em 2028.

Trump não estará novamente na cédula e, embora possa continuar fazendo campanha pelo partido, não há um sucessor claro ou evidente que consiga mobilizar a base como ele.

Em entrevistas à BBC, participantes da convenção frequentemente olhavam para a eleição daqui a dois anos e discutiam quem deveria ser o sucessor de Trump.

O vice-presidente J.D. Vance e o secretário de Estado Marco Rubio foram mencionados com frequência como principais candidatos.

Trump, no entanto, deixou claro em Dallas que ainda está no comando e não tem pressa de abrir mão dos holofotes.

Mais cedo, na quarta-feira, enquanto partia para a convenção, Trump reconheceu que os americanos talvez tenham de esperar mais algum tempo para terem algum alívio nos altos preços dos combustíveis.

"Acho que vai demorar um pouco mais do que as eleições de meio de mandato", disse Trump.

O presidente repetiu essa mensagem em seu discurso, argumentando que a dor econômica de curto prazo causada pela guerra no Irã valia a pena para impedir Teerã de desenvolver armas nucleares.

"Acho que a guerra vai acabar logo após a eleição, porque eles não aguentam mais", disse Trump sobre Teerã na quarta-feira.

Ele acrescentou que o Irã estava "desesperado para tentar influenciar a eleição, de modo que pudéssemos colocar lá um belo grupo de pessoas fracas" — uma aparente referência aos democratas — "e deixá-los em paz, permitindo que tivessem sua arma nuclear".

Mas essa pode ser uma mensagem difícil de transmitir a eleitores que sentem o impacto dos preços mais altos.

Pesquisas têm indicado de forma consistente nos últimos meses que o custo de vida é uma das principais questões para os americanos.

A taxa de aprovação de Trump também foi afetada à medida que a guerra no Irã se prolongou.

Uma pesquisa do jornal Financial Times / Focaldata divulgada no domingo indicou que esta aprovação atingiu uma nova mínima, com apenas 33% dos eleitores registrados aprovando seu desempenho como presidente.

Muitos candidatos republicanos podem ter esperado uma mensagem mais direta sobre como lidar com o custo de vida e encerrar rapidamente a guerra no Irã.

Trump costuma lançar ideias pouco convencionais em comícios.

Na noite de quarta-feira, isso tomou a forma de uma oferta para pagar US$ 5 mil (cerca de R$ 25,5 mil) a cada cidadão americano adulto caso os republicanos vençam nas duas Casas do Congresso em novembro.

A única condição, disse Trump, era que o dinheiro teria de ser gasto nos EUA.

Ele não deu detalhes sobre como o plano funcionaria, de onde viria o dinheiro ou como o governo dos EUA monitoraria como desse dinheiro seria gasto.

Os democratas rapidamente classificaram a proposta como "promessa vazia", e outros questionaram se tal compromisso seria sequer legal.

Há quase 270 milhões de adultos americanos, o que significa que um pagamento de US$ 5 mil custaria ao governo dos EUA cerca de US$ 1,3 trilhão (R$ 6,6 trilhões).

A possibilidade ou não do plano ser viável pareceu ser irrelevante. A ideia foi recebida com aplausos entusiasmados na convenção, e Trump pareceu aproveitar o momento.

articles.title: Alerta de tempestade no Vale do Paraíba: ventos de 100 km/h e granizo | G1
articles.standfirst: Aviso de perigo vale até 23h59 desta quinta-feira (10) e prevê chuva de até 100 mm por dia, ventos de até 100 km/h e queda de granizo.
articles.summary: O alerta de tempestade no Vale do Paraíba prevê chuvas intensas, granizo e ventos de 100 km/h com risco de alagamentos e quedas de árvores até o fim desta quinta-feira.
articles.body:
O Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) emitiu um alerta de perigo para tempestades que abrange áreas do Vale do Paraíba, região bragantina, Serra da Mantiqueira e Litoral Norte de São Paulo nesta quinta-feira (10).

O aviso começou às 8h55 e é válido até 23h59. A previsão indica chuva de 30 a 60 mm por hora ou de até 100 mm no dia, além de ventos de 60 a 100 km/h e possibilidade de queda de granizo.

O alerta indica risco de alagamentos, queda de árvores, interrupção no fornecimento de energia elétrica e danos em plantações.

Durante as tempestades, a recomendação é evitar ficar debaixo de árvores por causa do risco de quedas e descargas elétricas. Também é indicado não estacionar veículos próximos a torres de transmissão e placas de propaganda.

Se possível, aparelhos elétricos e o quadro geral de energia devem ser desligados durante a ocorrência de raios e ventos fortes.

Em caso de emergência, a Defesa Civil atende pelo telefone 199 e o Corpo de Bombeiros pelo 193.

articles.title: Escola municipal fica sem energia após furto, em São José | G1
articles.standfirst: Caso aconteceu na Escola Municipal Professora Luiza Maria Cavalcanti Guratti, no Jardim Setville.
articles.summary: Caso aconteceu na Escola Municipal Professora Luiza Maria Cavalcanti Guratti, no Jardim Setville.
articles.body:
Escola municipal fica sem energia após furto, em São José — Foto: Pedro Melo/TV Vanguarda

Uma escola municipal de São José dos Campos amanheceu sem energia nesta quinta-feira (10), após os fios serem furtados.

O caso aconteceu na Escola Municipal Professora Luiza Maria Cavalcanti Guratti, no Jardim Setville. Ela funciona em tempo integral.

Segundo apuração da TV Vanguarda , os fios de um poste-padrão foram cortados no alto. Os conduítes também foram quebrados e algumas partes deles ficaram no chão da escola.

Além dos alunos, professores também foram prejudicados com a falta de energia. Funcionários da Urbam foram até o local para fazer a manutenção na fiação, mas ainda seria necessário o reparo pela concessionária de energia.

De acordo com a Prefeitura de São José dos Campos, o caso aconteceu durante a madrugada e a Guarda Civil Municipal foi acionada. A administração informou ainda que uma equipe técnica da Secretaria de Educação e Cidadania foi enviada à escola antes do início das aulas e que ela acompanha os serviços de manutenção de energia e o atendimento aos alunos.

articles.title: EUA parabenizaram mais de 180 países em 12 meses; Brasil ficou de fora | G1
articles.standfirst: Governo Trump fez comunicados sobre feriados de independência e até de padroeira. Levantamento leva em consideração comunicados do Departamento de Estado ou de embaixadas dos EUA.
articles.summary: Governo Trump fez comunicados sobre feriados de independência e até de padroeira. Levantamento leva em consideração comunicados do Departamento de Estado ou de embaixadas dos EUA.
articles.body:
O Departamento de Estado dos Estados Unidos não publicou, pelo segundo ano consecutivo, um comunicado em homenagem ao Dia da Independência do Brasil, celebrado na segunda-feira (7). A prática é usada pelo governo americano para parabenizar países pelo "Dia Nacional" , que pode marcar desde aniversários de independência até a celebração de uma padroeira.

Um levantamento feito pelo g1 com base em comunicados publicados no site do Departamento de Estado apontou que, nos últimos 12 meses, os EUA enviaram parabéns a governos ou povos de mais de 180 países. O Brasil aparece ao lado de outras nove nações que ficaram de fora.

Além do Brasil, o governo norte-americano também não publicou comunicados para Afeganistão, Coreia do Norte, Etiópia, Guiné, Irã, Líbia, Santa Lúcia, Síria e Sudão .

A última vez que os EUA publicaram um comunicado parabenizando o Brasil pelo Dia da Independência foi em 2024 , durante o governo do presidente Joe Biden.

À época, o então secretário de Estado, Antony Blinken, assinou uma nota com "saudações calorosas" ao povo brasileiro.

"Que os anos vindouros continuem a fortalecer nossos laços e nossos valores democráticos compartilhados. Os Estados Unidos desejam ao povo brasileiro uma feliz celebração do Dia da Independência", dizia a nota.

Mas o tom mudou após o presidente Donald Trump voltar à Casa Branca, em janeiro de 2025. Desde então, as relações diplomáticas entre Brasil e Estados Unidos se deterioraram e entraram em uma crise com a aplicação de tarifas e sanções por parte do governo norte-americano.

📄 O g1 perguntou ao Itamaraty se os EUA haviam enviado algum comunicado ao governo brasileiro. O Ministério das Relações Exteriores orientou a reportagem a buscar o governo norte-americano. Já o Departamento de Estado não respondeu a um pedido de comentário.

É comum que os Estados Unidos publiquem notas públicas sobre o "Dia Nacional" de um país amigo. No último ano, o governo Trump comemorou até mesmo datas importantes de países com relações conturbadas, como Rússia, China e Venezuela.

Na terça-feira (8), por exemplo, o Departamento de Estado enviou felicitações a Andorra , que fica entre a Espanha e a França. Na data, o país celebra o Dia de Nossa Senhora de Meritxell, padroeira de Andorra e feriado que corresponde ao Dia Nacional do país.

"Enquanto o povo de Andorra celebra este dia importante, os Estados Unidos reafirmam sua parceria com o Principado e estendem seus mais calorosos cumprimentos ao povo andorrano no próximo ano", diz a nota assinada pelo secretário de Estado, Marco Rubio.

👉 Veja no mapa abaixo os países que os EUA parabenizaram nos últimos 12 meses:

Parabéns dos EUA nos últimos 12 meses, entre setembro de 2025 e setembro de 2026 — Foto: Gui Sousa/g1

No caso de Bahamas, Iêmen, Israel e Tunísia , não foi localizado nenhum comunicado do Departamento de Estado. Apesar disso, as embaixadas dos EUA nesses países fizeram posts sobre as datas nas redes sociais.

Sobre Cuba , o secretário Marco Rubio publicou uma nota e um vídeo diretamente dirigidos ao povo cubano, nos quais reafirma "o apoio inabalável dos Estados Unidos ao povo cubano em sua busca por liberdade, dignidade e autodeterminação".

Em relação à Líbia , a mídia local afirmou em janeiro que Trump enviou uma carta ao presidente Mohamed Menfi parabenizando-o pelo aniversário da independência. No entanto, o g1 não encontrou manifestações públicas do governo dos EUA.

O levantamento levou em consideração publicações feitas entre 10 de setembro de 2025 e esta quarta-feira (9).

Trump e Lula durante encontro na Casa Branca, em 7 de maio de 2026 — Foto: Presidência da República

As relações entre Brasil e Estados Unidos começaram a se deteriorar em julho do ano passado, quando Trump anunciou tarifas sobre produtos brasileiros importados pelos americanos.

Na época, o presidente dos EUA justificou o tarifaço pelo que chamou de "caça às bruxas" contra o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro.

Nos meses seguintes, negociações entre o governo brasileiro e a Casa Branca ajudaram a reduzir as tensões.

No fim de 2025, os EUA aliviaram as tarifas e retiraram algumas sanções contra autoridades brasileiras.

Além disso, Lula e Trump se encontraram duas vezes. O presidente brasileiro visitou Washington em 7 de maio para se reunir com o líder americano, que chegou a elogiar o petista.

No entanto, a relação entre os dois países voltou a se desgastar no fim de maio, quando os EUA classificaram as facções brasileiras Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) e Comando Vermelho (CV) como organizações terroristas .

A decisão foi anunciada dias após o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), candidato à Presidência da República, se reunir com Trump e com o secretário Marco Rubio nos Estados Unidos.

Semanas depois, os EUA anunciaram novas tarifas contra o Brasil. Em 22 de julho, entrou em vigor uma taxa de 25% como resultado de uma investigação aberta com base na Seção 301 da Lei de Comércio.

A medida foi anunciada após o governo Trump concluir que o Brasil adota práticas que "oneram ou restringem" o comércio com os EUA. Entre os exemplos citados estão o sistema de pagamentos PIX e a regulação de plataformas digitais.

Dois dias depois, os EUA confirmaram outra tarifa, de 12,5%, contra o Brasil e dezenas de outros países. O governo americano alegou práticas comerciais desleais relacionadas à falta de combate ao trabalho forçado .

Ainda em 24 de julho, o Itamaraty negou vistos a dois diplomatas do Departamento de Estado que viajariam ao Brasil: o secretário-assistente Riley M. Barnes e o subsecretário-assistente Samuel Samson.

Os dois foram citados em reportagem do jornal The Washington Post como responsáveis por uma estratégia para questionar a integridade e a confiabilidade do sistema eleitoral brasileiro.

Um porta-voz do Departamento de Estado negou que os funcionários pretendiam interferir nas eleições.

Segundo os EUA, a visita tinha como objetivo discutir "integridade eleitoral, liberdade religiosa e liberdade de expressão" com autoridades brasileiras e representantes da sociedade civil.

Sem acordo com Brasil, EUA impuseram tarifas de 25% contra alguns produtos — Foto: Joao Oliveira/Zoonar/picture alliance

Em agosto, o visto da embaixadora do Brasil em Washington foi revogad o. Segundo o Departamento de Estado, a medida foi uma resposta à demora das autoridades brasileiras em conceder o aval diplomático para que Daniel Perez assuma a embaixada dos EUA no Brasil.

Perez foi indicado ao cargo de embaixador dos EUA no Brasil em junho . Segundo o blog da Ana Flor , a indicação dele causou mal-estar no governo brasileiro porque o anúncio foi feito antes de uma consulta reservada às autoridades brasileiras.

Tradicionalmente, a nomeação de um embaixador só é anunciada após o país anfitrião sinalizar que aceita a indicação.

No caso de Perez, o pedido de aval foi feito ao governo brasileiro mais de duas semanas após o anúncio da indicação pela Casa Branca.

Em nota divulgada à época, o Itamaraty repudiou a decisão americana e disse que as justificativas apresentadas pelo Departamento de Estado são "falsas".

"[A medida] Faz parte de uma escalada deliberada de medidas hostis ao Brasil, motivadas por razões ideológicas incompatíveis com uma parceria bilateral que sempre foi pautada pelo respeito mútuo", afirmou.

"Fica óbvio também o interesse descabido de interferir na próxima eleição para presidente."

Em uma entrevista no fim do mês passado, Perez afirmou que não irá se envolver nas eleições presidenciais de outubro. Ele também disse que irá trabalhar para que Brasil e EUA alcancem um acordo comercial que seja benéfico para os dois países.

articles.title: Incêndio atinge prédio em Candeias; vídeo mostra chamas em apartamento | G1
articles.standfirst: Mulher morava com dois filhos no local e contou que um curto-circuito provocou o fogo. Ninguém ficou ferido, segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, que enviou quatro viaturas.
articles.summary: Mulher morava com dois filhos no local e contou que um curto-circuito provocou o fogo. Ninguém ficou ferido, segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, que enviou quatro viaturas.
articles.body:
Um incêndio atingiu um apartamento no 5º andar de um prédio no bairro de Candeias, em Jaboatão dos Guararapes , no Grande Recife , na madrugada desta quinta-feira (10). Não houve feridos, segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, que enviou quatro viaturas para o edifício na Avenida Abdo Cabus. Imagens enviadas para a TV Globo mostram as chamas no local ( veja vídeo acima ).

O incêndio aconteceu por volta das 3h e vizinhos utilizaram extintores de incêndio para tentar apagar as chamas antes da chegada dos bombeiros. Uma mulher com dois filhos morava no apartamento atingido pelo fogo e contou que um curto-circuito num ventilador provocou o incêndio.

A moradora, que não teve o nome divulgado, também afirmou que acordou com o cheiro de fumaça e tirou os filhos do apartamento, além de bater na porta dos vizinhos para avisar do incêndio.

Em nota, o Corpo de Bombeiros informou que as equipes realizaram o combate às chamas e a evacuação dos andares superiores. A corporação militar também declarou que os outros apartamentos do prédio não foram atingidos pelo incêndio.

De acordo com Rodrigo Reis, um morador que reside no mesmo prédio, o gás do edifício foi desligado, e os vizinhos do andar de cima do apartamento precisaram sair do apartamento e só podem retornar ao imóvel no fim da tarde desta quinta-feira.

articles.title: Temporal com rajadas de vento deixa quase 30 mil clientes sem energia no Paraná; saiba como acionar a Copel  | G1
articles.standfirst: Companhia mobiliza equipes para restabelecer fornecimento. Região Oeste concentra o maior número de desligamentos, com 12 mil unidades afetadas.
articles.summary: Companhia mobiliza equipes para restabelecer fornecimento. Região Oeste concentra o maior número de desligamentos, com 12 mil unidades afetadas.
articles.body:
Um forte temporal com rajadas de vento atingiu o Paraná entre a noite de quarta-feira (9) e a madrugada desta quinta-feira (10) e deixou cerca de 29,9 mil clientes sem energia em todas as regiões do estado.

A Companhia Paranaense de Energia (Copel) informou que equipes estão mobilizadas para restabelecer o fornecimento.

Segundo a companhia, os trabalhos de recomposição da rede são dinâmicos, e o número de interrupções tende a diminuir conforme os reparos avançam.

A região Oeste concentra o maior número de unidades consumidoras sem luz, com 12 mil. Em seguida aparecem a Região Metropolitana de Curitiba e o Litoral, com 6,5 mil, e o Noroeste, com 6,4 mil.

O Centro-Sul soma 2,4 mil unidades sem energia, o Sudoeste, 2,1 mil, e o Norte, 350.

Queda de árvores e alagamentos foram registrados em Terra Roxa — Foto: Júlio Simões de Lima

Apaixonada por viagens, mãe amorosa: Quem era a médica encontrada morta em apartamento

Qualquer pessoa pode registrar o problema pela internet, por SMS ou pelo aplicativo da companhia. Registro é feito na hora.

A Companhia Paranaense de Energia (Copel) disponibiliza três canais para que clientes comunicarem falta de energia: internet, mensagem de texto (SMS) e aplicativo. O serviço pode ser usado por qualquer pessoa, e o registro da ocorrência é feito na hora.

Basta acessar o site da Copel, clicar em "Consultar" e informar o número da Unidade Consumidora ou o CPF.

Quem preferir enviar mensagem de texto deve mandar um SMS para o número 28593, digitando as letras "SL" seguidas do número da Unidade Consumidora — apenas números, com o dígito verificador, sem pontos ou hífen. O envio é gratuito.

O app da Copel está disponível para iPhone, na App Store, e para Android, na Play Store. Após baixar o aplicativo, é preciso aceitar os termos de uso e informar CPF e senha. Quem for usar o serviço pela primeira vez deve selecionar a opção "Novo cadastro". Depois de fazer login, a falta de energia pode ser comunicada na página inicial, na opção "Informar falta de luz".

articles.title: MCD continues demolition drive against unsafe, illegal buildings after deadly building collapse
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) continued its demolition and enforcement drive against dangerous buildings, unauthorised construct.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) continued its demolition and enforcement drive against dangerous buildings, unauthorised construction and violations of building norms across all 12 zones of the national capital on Thursday, days after the collapse of a paying guest accommodation in Satya Niketan killed seven people and injured at least five.Visuals from areas including Laxmi Nagar, Jagatpuri and Pandav Nagar showed civic teams carrying out demolition and enforcement action against structures found to be in violation of building norms.Over the last 2-3 days, MCD teams also carried out action in Vishwas Nagar, Mukherjee Nagar, Jamia Nagar, Shaheen Bagh, Tilak Nagar, Karam Pura, Karol Bagh, Ramesh Nagar, Mansarovar Garden, Chandni Chowk and Nehru Vihar, with the drive expected to continue there.Meanwhile, the MCD resumed controlled demolition of the building adjoining the one that collapsed in Satya Niketan on September 6. Officials said the structure was being demolished in a calibrated manner.The ongoing drive is part of a wider crackdown across Delhi on unauthorised construction, illegal misuse of properties and structurally unsafe buildings, which has intensified following the Satya Niketan collapse.As part of a safety assessment exercise launched after the incident, the MCD surveyed 1,252 paying guest (PG) buildings between September 7 and 9.Official records show that between June 1 and September 9, the civic body carried out 1,053 demolition actions, sealed 491 properties and issued 2,316 show-cause notices and 757 demolition notices as part of its enforcement drive across the city.(With inputs from PTI)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Manipur's Chongtham Vikram Singh: The rock guitarist whose killing shocked India's north-east
articles.summary: A renowned Manipuri guitarist's killing has sparked anger - and an outpouring of memories about his life and music.
articles.body:
When Chongtham Vikram Singh finally came home to India's north-eastern state of Manipur, his old friend Dhiren Sadokpam went to the airport to receive him.

It was not the homecoming he had imagined. Vikram arrived in the cargo hold, inside a coffin.

Three days earlier, the 54-year-old musician had been beaten to death outside his home in south-east Delhi.

"Nobody seemed to have the strength to speak," Sadokpam told the BBC. "What could be said?"

Vikram had spent much of his life travelling with his guitars, carrying his music from small stages in Manipur's capital, Imphal, to jazz clubs, classrooms and concert halls in Delhi.

According to police and his family, he had gone downstairs late on Sunday night after a group of men were shouting and drinking outside his apartment building. When he objected to the disturbance, the men allegedly attacked him.

His wife, Joshna Chongtham, said Vikram returned upstairs but was pursued and assaulted outside the family's apartment.

Hours later, after complaining of breathlessness, he was taken to hospital by his 20-year-old son. He died there early in the morning.

Seven men and a juvenile have been arrested in connection with his killing. Police say they are investigating the circumstances of the attack.

The death has prompted an outpouring of grief and anger, and renewed concerns about the discrimination faced by people from India's north-east in Delhi, where members of the community have for years reported racial abuse, harassment and violence.

Police say they have so far found no evidence of a racial motive. But north-eastern groups have held protests and demanded an impartial investigation.

The case has also drawn attention to Vikram himself - a familiar figure in Manipur's music scene who, over four decades of playing and teaching, gathered around him a large circle of students, friends and admirers.

At a press conference two days after his death, his wife Joshna said: "We are not seeking revenge. We are seeking justice. He had a name, a family and a life that mattered."

For most of his 54 years, that life had revolved around music.

Vikram grew up around it. His mother, Chongtham Kamala, was a celebrated singer who lent her voice to Matamgi Manipur, the first feature film made in the Manipuri language.

As a boy, he accompanied her to All India Radio for recordings. Before long, he had auditioned there himself and become a child artist, playing the accordion.

There is an old black-and-white photograph of Vikram from those years. He is kneeling stiffly in front of a microphone with an accordion balanced across his lap. Beside him, another boy sits behind a pair of drums. Both wear the grave expressions of children who have been told that a photograph is being taken.

The boy with the accordion would soon discover guitars - first Hawaiian and Spanish, then electric - and, somewhere along the way, acquire thick black glasses and a splendid moustache.

By the mid-1980s, Imphal had become an unlikely outpost of rock music. The sound travelled there largely on cassette tapes, bringing with it the hard rock and heavy metal being played thousands of miles away.

Young men formed bands and crowded into local halls, working with whatever they could find - modest sound systems, locally made amplifiers, guitars turned up as loud as they would go. They listened, copied, experimented.

Vikram was studying at Don Bosco School then and still playing accordion and Hawaiian guitar. Years later, he remembered how he and his friends would ask the priests for permission to leave school to watch a local band perform.

"Those were sweet and innocent days that actually inspired me to go for rock," he recalled in a 2014 interview .

Soon, watching was no longer enough. Vikram took up the electric guitar and began playing in bands himself - first Ultra Vires, then Phoenix and Eastern Dark - becoming part of the generation that was giving Imphal's new rock scene a sound of its own.

It was around this time, in 1987, that Dhiren Sadokpam first met him.

They were setting off from Imphal to study in Shillong, and Sadokpam remembers them waiting at a temporary interstate bus terminal with backpacks, steel luggage boxes and bedding for the long journey.

Vikram was boyish and energetic, he recalls, but mostly kept to himself.

"He would spend long hours in his room, mastering each and every composition that came his way," Sadokpam said.

With each band, Vikram's playing evolved. Ultra Vires became a place to experiment. Phoenix, which would become one of the defining bands of Manipur's early rock scene, brought greater precision and a devoted following that endured long after its heyday.

By the time he joined Eastern Dark, Sadokpam remembers the quiet young man disappearing into the instrument, making its six strings "cry and sing".

In the early 1990s, he spent two years in Calcutta (now Kolkata), where he encountered musicians at the Calcutta School of Music, a century-old institution with a strong tradition of Western classical music, and was drawn more deeply into jazz and classical music. His own playing began to range across styles, from rock and blues to jazz and fusion.

By the 2000s, Vikram had moved to Delhi, where he built a life around performing and teaching music.

In 2010, he reconnected with an old musician friend and formed Fubar Ghetto. The band played jazz, blues, rock and fusion, with improvisation at the centre of it. Their first performance was a charity concert near the Yamuna river.

From there, they worked their way through Delhi's live-music circuit: universities, clubs and cultural festivals, the National School of Drama and, on one occasion, the Czech Embassy.

Vikram never became a major star. Instead, he built the quieter reputation of a working musician - among the people he played with, the students he taught and the musicians he helped along the way.

Since his killing, many of those people have remembered the man who was gentle, generous and largely uninterested in recognition.

Former student guitarist Sachidananda Angom remembered him as "always kind, helpful" and someone who "could really light up a room", reported The Indian Express.

Mame Khan, the Rajasthani folk singer with whom Vikram performed for several years, told The Indian Express that Vikram was "a really kind and lovely person" who never picked arguments with anyone.

Sadokpam is careful not to make more of their friendship than it was.

They had met as young men in 1987, lost touch for two decades and found each other again in middle age. In between, Sadokpam followed Vikram's musical life from a distance, as a fan and a friend.

They last met in Delhi in 2019, when Vikram invited him home for dinner.

"Vikram picked up his guitar and played and spoke excitedly about his students," he recalled.

When it was time to leave, Vikram asked him to come again soon. Sadokpam said he promised he would.

articles.title: In 1816, Kentucky Shakers built a dwelling where newcomers learned about the community; the last surviving North Lot building is now getting a $1.5M restoration to reopen by 2029
articles.summary: US News: Shaker believers in Mercer County began dismantling a frame house on December 16, 1816, to build a new dwelling about a mile northeast of their villag.
articles.body: Shaker believers in Mercer County began dismantling a frame house on December 16, 1816, to build a new dwelling about a mile northeast of their village centre. The move was deliberate. The Shaker community was growing, and they needed a proper place for new converts to live and learn about Shaker life. The new building welcomed seekers, those who were curious about the doctrines of Mother Ann Lee, the founder of the community. For over a century, the North Lot Family Dwelling served as a place where people decided whether to join the community.Two centuries later, that building stands nearly empty, its structural integrity compromised by decades of neglect. However, Kentucky's preservation community has decided that it deserves a resurrection. A $1.5 million restoration has begun, and by 2029, the North Lot Family Dwelling will reopen, this time as a gathering space for different reasons, of course.An 1816 dwelling gets a second lifeThe 210-year-old Shaker building that once served as a home for newcomers is being restored in a $1.5 million project, with plans to welcome visitors again by 2029. Shaker Village has received a $750,000 federal grant through the Save America's Treasures programme from the Historic Preservation Fund, administered by the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior, to support the restoration of the historic North Lot Family Dwelling, one of the most significant structures within the Village's 3,000-acre National Historic Landmark.“This is a transformative moment for Shaker Village,” Billy Rankin, Shaker Village President & CEO, said in a press release. “The North Lot Family Dwelling tells a powerful story about how the Shakers formed their community and connected with their fellow Kentuckians throughout the 19th century. Restoring this building allows that story to be shared in a way that has never been possible before. Plus, it will act as the ‘front porch’ of the Village since its placement along historic Highway 68 is the first Shaker structure many see when approaching the Village.”The building is currently at risk due to structural and water damage. The restoration will be done via a three-phase approach, which includes structural repairs, masonry and exterior restoration, and full upgrades to mechanical systems.The total restoration will cost an estimated $1.5 million. The federal grant has been matched by funding from the Team Kentucky GRANT Program, private donor contributions, and in-kind support from Shaker Village's preservation team. The restoration will be complete within three years, with plans to reopen the North Lot Family Dwelling in 2029.What the North Lot once representedThe Shaker settlement at Pleasant Hill grew rapidly in the early 1800s. New converts arrived in waves, drawn by reports of successful communal farming, orderly worship, and a faith that promised salvation through confession and celibacy. The community needed intake stations. Housing was scarce, but inviting newcomers into established family units was not an option. So they built several dwellings, and the North Lot became one of two gathering orders at Pleasant Hill, a place where visitors could apprentice in communal life before choosing permanent membership. People who chose to commit were moved to the village, into one of the larger family dwellings that still dot the 3,000-acre landscape today.The North Lot once had about a dozen buildings. Many lived, worked, and followed their spiritual paths there. While some converted, others left. This North Lot building, now awaiting a second life, is the only one standing. It is a three-storey timber-frame building that had five bedrooms, a full kitchen, and a large sitting area that doubled as meeting space.Families lived, worked, and assessed their spiritual readiness there. Some converted. Many left. The building that survives was three storeys, with sturdy timber-frame construction, designed to accommodate a rotating population of uncertain believers. This is where the newcomers experienced Shaker routines like communal meals, work assignments, and worship practices. The building functioned as both residence and classroom.By the time Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill acquired the North Lot property in 1966, the Shaker community at Pleasant Hill had long since ceased to operate as a religious community. In the late 1970s, restoration began and was completed in 1981. From the following year, the building hosted retreats, guests, and small groups in a quiet setting. This arrangement lasted until 2008. That's when U.S. Highway 68 effectively erased the North Lot from the visitor experience. The building was later closed, and maintenance was neglected. By 2016, the building was in serious disrepair and at risk of further deterioration.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1951, an artist and a librarian built a riverside cabin with no electricity and lived from the land for 35 years; their 61-acre homestead is now being preserved
articles.summary: US News: Discover the extraordinary story of Harlan and Anna Hubbard, who lived off the land for 35 years in their riverside cabin. Learn about the preservation of their 61-acre homestead along the Ohio River.
articles.body: Harlan and Anna Hubbard settled beside the Ohio River in Kentucky in 1951 after traveling by shantyboat for years. The following year, they began building the small cabin that became Payne Hollow, which is a home where they lived with few modern conveniences and relied heavily on the surrounding land and river.Harlan Hubbard was an artist, writer and craftsman, and Anna was a librarian and musician. Together they developed a life around the property in Trimble County, Kentucky, and grew food, gathered wood and made much of what they needed themselves. Historical records place the cabin’s construction in 1952, after the Hubbards had negotiated for land at Payne's Landing. A University of Louisville-related historical account says they returned to the site in May 1952, arranged to rent and later purchase seven acres, and moved into a one-room cabin by November that year. The structure expanded into a two-room home in 1954.They built a life around the riverThe Hubbards built their shantyboat in 1944 and traveled along the Ohio and Mississippi river system before settling at the Kentucky site, and at Payne Hollow, the couple continued the same basic approach to daily life. Hanover College's account of the property says that they rejected modern conveniences and lived without electricity or running water, while relying on the land around their home.Harlan painted, wrote and produced woodcuts, and often used materials and subjects connected to the Ohio River landscape. He is credited with more than 1,000 works of art. Anna was a librarian and musician, and the couple's life included music as well as Harlan's painting and writing. They remained at Payne Hollow for more than three decades. Anna died in 1986, while Harlan died in 1988. By then, the property had become closely associated with their work and the self-sufficient life they had created there. Hanover College says the couple's riverside property eventually encompassed 61 acres, including the buildings and their contents.The property passed to a caretakerThe 61-acre Payne Hollow property went to Paul Hassfurder, an artist who had become a close friend of the Hubbards and helped them during their later years, after Harlan's death. Hassfurder moved into the house shortly after Harlan died and continued living there in much the same spirit as the couple. Earlier accounts of Payne Hollow describe him maintaining the property and resisting major changes that could have altered its character.Payne Hollow sits along the Ohio River in Trimble County, downstream from Madison, Indiana, and access has historically involved the river and a wooded route rather than the kind of infrastructure that is associated with conventional residential development. The property remained closely associated with Hubbard's artwork and writing, while concerns about the condition of its buildings grew. Preservationists were already discussing ways to protect the house, studio and surrounding land by the 2000s.A nonprofit took over the 61 acresThe preservation effort entered a new phase in 2022, when a nonprofit organization named Payne Hollow in Ohio acquired the 61-acre property. The organization was established to preserve the land and structures and to develop educational and research uses around the Hubbard legacy. Hanover College reported that the group planned to stabilize the buildings, safeguard historically significant artifacts and conduct ecological work on the property.The organization has described the site as a work in progress, and its own account says the house and studio are deteriorating and need restoration, while recent photographs document the property as it exists today. The organization is also documenting the surrounding land, trails and ecological features while developing plans for future stewardship.When Hanover College reported on the acquisition in 2022, Payne Hollow was closed to the public while the nonprofit developed its preservation and access plans. The property had moved from private inheritance into the hands of an organization specifically created to maintain the land, buildings and collection that were associated with Harlan and Anna Hubbard.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Uganda's King Oyo death: Royal family rejects UBC presenter Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma as the new monarch
articles.summary: King Oyo's family say he left a will naming his young son as heir to the Tooro kingdom.
articles.body:
A bitter succession dispute has erupted in one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms, days before the burial of its late king, who until his death had been the world's youngest reigning monarch.

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who ruled the Tooro Kingdom for more than three decades, was undergoing cancer treatment in the US when he died last month aged 34 .

Royal clan elders have named popular TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56, as the next monarch, but this has been rejected by Oyo's close family.

His sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, said the late king had left a will written in 2022 naming his young son, whose identity has never been disclosed, as his successor.

"My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday night of creating "confusion and turmoil" while the family was still grieving.

Meanwhile the late king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, has said royal guards have been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed, restricting the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing the situation as "house arrest".

She appealed to the army's leadership and President Yoweri Museveni to allow the family to mourn and bury Oyo in peace on Saturday.

"I appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."

Thousands of mourners are expected to attend the burial at the royal tombs near the palace in Fort Portal in western Uganda.

His body was returned to Uganda from the US on Friday , and preparations for the funeral are under way.

Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. Its monarch has no formal political authority but remains an important cultural figure in western Uganda.

Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967, but they were restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.

The existence of Oyo's son was first publicly revealed in the days after the king's death by President Museveni, who said he had been told about the young boy by the queen mother.

No other details have officially been disclosed, and he had not previously been presented as Oyo's heir.

The disagreement has exposed the complicated way in which succession works in Tooro.

Unlike Britain's monarchy, where the crown passes according to an established line of succession, Tooro's monarch is chosen from the Babiito, the royal dynastic clan.

At a press conference in ​the kingdom's capital of Fort Portal, the royal clan's succession committee announced Kijanangoma, Oyo's cousin and a news presenter ​at the state-run broadcaster UBC, as monarch.

The clan elders said they had the customary authority to choose a suitable prince to become "the Omukama" - the local title for the king of Tooro.

The succession panel said it had carried out "due diligence, consultation and adequate consideration" before selecting Kijanangoma, with 19 members signing the resolution.

Kijanangoma is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of former Tooro king George David Rukidi III.

Another royal, UK-based Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, was initially considered for the throne but declined, citing other responsibilities, according to the succession committee.

It is not yet clear when the enthronement will take place, but the committee said it would be conducted in accordance with the traditions and customs of the Tooro kingdom.

Oyo's family quickly called a press conference to denounce the announcement, insisting the late king's written wishes should be respected.

Princess Komuntale said Oyo had left "very strict instructions" on his succession, naming his son as first in line and also setting out alternatives if the boy could not take the throne - a position backed by her aunt, senior royal Princess Elizabeth Bagaaya.

But clan representatives said that reports of Oyo having a son were not sufficient because the child had not been formally presented to the royal clan as dictated by Tooro tradition.

One committee member told Uganda's NTV station that a royal child must be formally introduced to elders and then must undergo ceremonies and others preparations if they were to be considered for future leadership.

Culture Minister Henry Tumukunde has stepped in to say he will be overseeing mediation efforts, with an outcome expected after consultations with President Museveni and cultural leaders.

articles.title: In Indonesia, communities packed dead branches between rows of bamboo in damaged coastal areas; the permeable barriers trapped sediment and helped mangroves return
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Indonesian communities are fighting coastal erosion and restoring mangrove forests using bamboo barriers that trap sediment, creating sustainable habitats for marine life.
articles.body: Indonesia has the greatest expanse of mangrove forest anywhere on Earth, which formerly meant its coastline was one of the best protected in the tropics. But in the last few decades, significant swaths of that forest have been removed to make way for shrimp and fish ponds, exposing swathes of Java and Sumatra to waves that earlier smashed harmlessly against extensive root systems. Villages that never had to worry about the sea began to witness it move steadily inland, graveyards, homes and fields lost to water that mangroves used to hold back.The obvious initial response, simply transplanting seedlings, continued failing. Saplings placed in soft, wet muck are washed away before they can take root, and a study of Philippine mangrove programmes published in Wetlands Ecology and Management found long-term survival rates for conventional replanting schemes as low as ten to twenty per cent. In the end, a more patient approach worked, one that followed how mangroves naturally colonise land rather than fighting the mud. Coastal engineers and community groups began to drive bamboo poles into the shallows and pack the gaps between with dead branches, creating a permeable barrier that allowed water to flow but slowed it enough to allow silt to settle out.Building barriers that work with the tide, not against itThere is a basic, deceptive logic to this design. A concrete seawall stops water completely. Sounds protective, but in soft coastal mud it backfires, because the wall sinks under its weight and the water it deflects just erodes the land next to it. A bamboo and brushwood barrier behaves differently. Tidal water runs through the gaps in the branches, but the structure slows the current enough for suspended mud to drop out of the water column rather than being pushed further inland. Over months and years, this trapped silt gradually raises the level of the seabed behind the barrier, producing circumstances similar enough to a natural mudflat that mangrove seeds carried in by the tide can settle, root and flourish without being swept away.Communities in Demak, on Java's northern coast, are the most documented example of this approach. According to Wetlands International, locals have built more than three kilometres of wave-calming structures along a 20-kilometre stretch of shoreline, creating the calm, sediment-filled conditions mangroves need to re-establish themselves. This case shows why the practice has expanded well beyond a single community, and the same basic concept has now been tried across river deltas from Vietnam to Indonesia.A technique that spread from village experiments to national policyWhat started as cottage industry experimentation has been researched in detail by coastal engineers with a view to finding out exactly how much wave energy these tiny structures could soak up and how far the design might be pushed. A study published in the journal Ecological Engineering documented how the approach, often called the Building with Nature method, was scaled up by the Indonesian government after early trials, with more than 20 kilometres of permeable dams constructed across Java, Sumatra, Sulawesi and Kalimantan between 2017 and 2019 alone. The same researchers note that success depends heavily on local site conditions and sustained maintenance rather than a fixed formula, a more measured contrast to the often poor survival rates of conventional planting schemes.Part of the reason the technology is appealing to policymakers is that it is cheap and uses resources already at hand in coastal towns. Bamboo is abundant and inexpensive throughout much of Indonesia, and branches that otherwise would be wasted become the very material that captures the mud needed for fresh mangrove development. In several documented cases, fishermen and farmers who agreed to convert part of their ponds back to mangrove have seen their fish and shrimp catches rebound as habitat returned, since the trees provide nursery grounds that many commercially valuable species depend on.Lessons for other shores confronting rising seasIncreasing sea levels and groundwater extraction are increasingly posing threats to coastal erosion in South and Southeast Asia, including areas of the eastern shoreline of India, where the cover of mangroves has also reduced drastically in the past few decades. The Indonesian example is a valuable reminder that not all coastal preservation needs to be expensive engineering and that patient, low-cost initiatives based on natural processes can occasionally do better than more costly options.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Baltimore kept an invasive pear as its official tree for 52 years; after Maryland banned its sale, six costumed native trees raced to reveal its replacement, the tulip poplar
articles.summary: US News: For 52 years, Baltimore had the Chanticleer pear, also known as the callery pear, as its official city tree. That changed last month after the city se.
articles.body: For 52 years, Baltimore had the Chanticleer pear, also known as the callery pear, as its official city tree. That changed last month after the city selected the tulip poplar as its new official tree, replacing a species whose sale was banned in Maryland earlier this year.The change was announced in an unusual way at Cylburn Arboretum. According to The Baltimore Banner, six native tree species from the Baltimore area competed for the title, with forestry staff dressed in elaborate tree costumes and racing around a track as hundreds of residents watched.The six finalists were the tulip poplar, American sycamore, blackgum, bald cypress, bitternut hickory and overcup oak. Residents had voted for their preferred tree during a months-long competition organised by Baltimore City Recreation and Parks.The public vote had already decided the winner, but the final announcement came through a footrace. Mayor Brandon Scott, who had described the contest as Baltimore’s “biggest race of the year,” started the event as the costumed trees ran for the finish line.Tulip poplar wins the raceThe American sycamore and bitternut hickory made strong starts, while the tall tulip poplar was near the back of the field. The bitternut hickory was shown carrying and dribbling a nut like a football.The race took another turn when a costumed callery pear suddenly appeared from a thicket and disrupted the contestants. The audience jeered the invasive pear as it eventually fell to the ground.The tulip poplar then tried to speed up in the final stretch but tripped over its own roots and collapsed. The American sycamore, played by forest ecologist Megan Carr, helped the fallen competitor get back on his feet.The tulip poplar soon recovered and overtook its helper before reaching the finish line. It crossed the tape about two and a half minutes after the race began, giving the species the title of Baltimore’s new official tree.Assistant chief forester Brendon Brown played the winning tulip poplar. After the race, he thanked the audience and Baltimore parks while speaking to an urban forester dressed as the Lorax, the Dr Seuss character who speaks for the forest.“I owe it all to my midwood,” Brown said, referring to a tree classification he had only recently discovered. He also thanked the fans and Baltimore parks, saying they support countless wildlife species.Why the pear was replacedThe callery pear had been Baltimore’s official tree since 1974, when former mayor William Donald Schaefer selected it because of its striking white blossoms and hardiness in city streets.But the tree later became associated with invasive growth. Maryland banned its sale earlier this year, ending its place as Baltimore’s official tree after more than five decades.Brown said he had actually voted for the blackgum rather than the tulip poplar. “I voted for blackgum,” he said. Still, he said the tulip poplar had several advantages. It is among the most common and tallest trees in many Baltimore parks.Megan Carr, who took part in the race dressed as an American sycamore, did not vote for the species she portrayed or for any of the other finalists. “How can you choose?” she said. “They are six wonderful trees.”A new tree for BaltimoreNot everyone at the event was happy about the change. Urban forester and certified nature therapy guide Teddy Martello dressed as the callery pear and defended the species. He described supporters of the native trees as “fascists” and said the pear had been unfairly criticised.Mayor Scott, however, showed little regret about removing Schaefer’s choice from its position. “That’s basically what my job has been since the day I got here,” Scott said. “Undoing all the bad things that they thought were good.”The tree contest was held during the summer gathering for TreeBaltimore, an initiative that has worked for two decades to increase the city’s tree canopy to 40%. Recent estimates, however, put Baltimore’s tree canopy at less than 28%.Urban forester Fred Chalfant, who attended the event dressed as the Lorax, had supported the overcup oak for the official tree title. He also praised the tulip poplar and said he was pleased by the public response. “I’m really excited about the turnout today and the enthusiasm for trees in Baltimore City,” Chalfant said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
