articles.title: In the year since we lost Charlie Kirk, the media has done its best to act its worst
articles.summary: From Jimmy Kimmel's suspension to Hasan Piker's mocking song, the year since Charlie Kirk's assassination unleashed a wave of media vitriol.
articles.body: It has already been a year since conservative icon Charlie Kirk was assassinated and the attack has brought out the worst in some of the worst people in our media and celebrity culture. False claims that the alleged assassin was conservative, false quotes and hateful comments have filled TV, radio and, of course, the internet. The world was scarred from the moment of the attack. Unedited video soon surfaced on social media and who knows how many watched someone they loved or admired get fatally shot. Instead of an outpouring of sympathy, we were transfixed by an endless parade of hate for Charlie, his widow Erika, conservatives and more. The hate came from all corners of the media and political world, including many names you know — then-MSNBC analyst Matthew Dowd, far-left podcaster Hasan Piker, multiple staffers at The Washington Post, longtime broadcaster Katie Couric and, of course, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel. Because if there’s something foul to say, Kimmel can’t be far from that gutter. Much of the commentary is so venomous or vomitous that I won’t dignify it by repeating what was said. Vile grifters have made mountains of cash attacking a grieving widow and I refuse to help them do it. REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR The left and media moved on quickly from the assassination to the character assassination of the victim. Charlie Kirk was bashed as "hateful," "bigoted," a "hatemonger" and a "prominent Christian nationalist" who "has been known to make racist statements." Even major news outlets fired or suspended some of those who bashed Kirk. But broadcast outlets did their best to hide the obvious connection between the alleged shooter and the left’s obsession that everyone on the right is "fascist." Kimmel was sidelined briefly for falsely claiming, "We hit some new lows over the weekend with the MAGA gang desperately trying to characterize this kid who murdered Charlie Kirk as anything other than one of them and doing everything they can to score political points from it." Kimmel later said his words were, "intentionally and, I think, maliciously mischaracterized." BOB IGER BREAKS SILENCE ON DISNEY'S SUSPENSION OF JIMMY KIMMEL OVER CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION COMMENTS The media, of course, supported him. MSNBC host Chris Hayes called the suspension, "the most straightforward attack on free speech from state actors I've ever seen in my life, and it's not even close." CNN media analyst Brian Stelter criticized the move, saying, "America is a less free place if late-night comedians cannot do or say what they want." CNN’s Jake Tapper headed up an hourlong special called "No Laughing Matter: Free Speech Under Attack" like ABC had done something wrong. As Tapper put it, "Less than 24 hours after Jimmy Kimmel was suspended, the tight-knit fraternity of late-night hosts rallied around their comedic brother." MSNBC’s Matthew Dowd lost his job for bashing Charlie Kirk, saying, "He’s been one of the most divisive, especially divisive, younger figures in this who has constantly sort of pushing this sort of hate speech or sort of aimed at certain groups and I always go back to hateful thoughts lead to hateful words, which then lead to hateful actions." Dowd later blamed "The right-wing media mob" for his firing. Of course. Longtime broadcaster Katie Couric blamed the victim. "I think some people might say Charlie Kirk's rhetoric was extreme." She added that some were "suggesting that these kinds of words lead to violence." Both major liberal newspapers joined in. Washington Post fashion reporter Ashley Fetters Maloy went after Erika Kirk for the clothes she was wearing and even her parenting under the headline: "Erika Kirk is walking a fine line in a glittering pantsuit." Maloy went on to raise two pathetic Post questions: "While you’re on this publicity tour, who’s parenting your kids?" and "Why is that suit so sparkly?" Making light of widows coping with loss is unsurprising for feminist journalists. As Erika commented, "If you are now attacking a widow's attire, like, that's where we're at." The Post was also ordered to reinstate bitter columnist Karen Attiah after she was fired last year for "gross misconduct" over social media posts she made after the assassination. "Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a White man that espoused violence is … not the same as violence," Attiah wrote. New York Times correspondent and 1619 Project author Nikole Hannah-Jones took a similar view, criticizing efforts "not just to condemn his killing and political violence, but to venerate him." She wrote this under a subhead whining about, "the mainstreaming of formerly extremist views." The paper also falsely accused Charlie of being antisemitic when, in reality, he was "quoting a statement from a post on social media and went on to critique it. It was not his own statement." The paper of record. Ugh. The lefty Atlantic actually wrote that "MAGA has found its George Floyd." Except, of course, that Charlie was an upstanding citizen and the right didn’t riot afterward. PETE DAVIDSON SPARKS BACKLASH AFTER EXPLICIT JOKE ABOUT SLAIN CHARLIE KIRK DURING NETFLIX ROAST Hollywood didn’t want to miss out on the hate fest. Former "Mean Girls" actress Amanda Seyfried called Charlie "hateful" and then flipped out because she got pushback. "I'm not f---ing apologizing for that," Seyfried later said. "Comedian" Pete Davidson made a disgusting gay joke about Charlie Kirk during Netflix’s "The Roast of Kevin Hart." But if you pay for Netflix, that’s the kind of high-class content you are supporting. Former "Daily Show" host Trevor Noah couldn’t get past how pro-Second Amendment Kirk "was shot while defending guns." He called it, "an incongruous funny thing that happens." "You are there. You're onstage, like, ‘Let me tell you why people should have guns.’ Wa-pow!" That’s the neutral individual who hosted the White House Correspondents' Dinner a couple years ago. HASAN PIKER SINGS MOCKING 'WE ARE CHARLIE KIRK' SONG AT LIVE PODCAST SHOW The podcasting world was its own unhinged pit of hate. Much of that I’m skipping and focusing on those the regular media still loves to interview and quote. Former sportscaster and MSNBC host Keith Olbermann complained that Sinclair broadcasting urged the FCC and ABC to do more than just suspend Kimmel. He had a typically measured response: "Burn in hell, Sinclair. Alongside Charlie Kirk." Loathsome podcasting harpy Jennifer Welch mocked Charlie. "The person that I heard that justified his death was him," Welch said. "He’s the one that said on tape that if school kids die, but it means he gets to have a Second Amendment, then that’s what it’s going to be. He’s the one that justified it." Far-left streamer Hasan Piker mockingly sang the song, "We Are Charlie Kirk" during a tour stop. Piker remains a media darling who hobnobs with top Democrats like Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and listing all of the other offensive things he has said would take much more space. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION But, despite all that we’ve seen in the past year, there is reason for hope. Even with a year’s worth of hate tossed around like grenades, that hope endures. I saw hundreds praying at a small north Georgia memorial service I attended. That was love, not hate. TV host Jenny McCarthy said the assassination inspired her in faith. "I’ve always been a follower of Christ, but when he passed, I completely surrendered," she said. "I am so devoted. I mean, I started Bible study immediately." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And Erika Kirk has shown her grace, her heart and her faith through all this. She had the courage to forgive the man who murdered her husband and I doubt seriously that many of us could do the same. Her husband Charlie made the world a better place for all that knew him or knew of him. And he’s still doing it. And that’s what the haters are most upset about. articles.title: ANDREW KOLVET: I spent eight years beside Charlie Kirk. Here’s what the world never understood
articles.summary: Andrew Kolvet reflects on Charlie Kirk's unlikely rise from a broke 18-year-old to building Turning Point USA and transforming the conservative movement.
articles.body: I first met Charlie Kirk in a hotel lobby in Los Angeles in 2017. I had emailed him a few times suggesting we should work together, and he mostly brushed me off or ignored the inquiries. I was doing communications work and had heard rumors of this young "up-and-comer" with "boundless energy" who was trying to take back college campuses for conservatives. After a bout of bad press, he finally replied and asked to meet, and as we shook hands that very first time, the first thing I noticed was just how tall he was! At 6’5", Charlie naturally towered over nearly everyone, but somehow his presence made him seem even larger. The next thing I remember were his eyes that seemed to dart all around the room. He managed to talk directly to you while also perceiving everything and everyone else around him simultaneously. He seemed to multitask by nature, a unique skill I would come to marvel at in years to come. REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR He was also very deliberate. You could tell that Charlie hated wasting time. Without being rude, he wanted to get right into the meat of the discussion, and as we talked, it was impossible not to notice his oversized suit, the dress shoes that seemed more appropriate for a 70-year-old man, or his overall Midwestern disdain for trends. But something about this 23-year-old kid was just, well, different. When he spoke, I believed him. In a political world full of talkers who put style above substance, Charlie was the opposite. I could tell he was willing to work his tail off. By the end of that meeting, we decided to work together, and thus a partnership and a friendship that would grow and expand over the next eight years began right then and there. That’s how Charlie worked. When he made up his mind, he moved. ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION In 2019, Charlie and I launched "The Charlie Kirk Show." It was supposed to be a once-a-week podcast — how could a man as busy as Charlie do more? But Charlie was always exceptional. Once a week morphed during COVID-19 into three, then five, then sometimes 10 episodes a week. Soon, it became a nationally syndicated radio program as well, and in 2022, it became a wildly successful television program. I have heard Charlie described in many ways over the last year, but one of my favorites comes from Blake Neff, one of our producers and a regular co-host. He describes Charlie as being the highest-agency person he’s ever known, and he’s right. Most people have great intentions, but Charlie possessed one of the rarest of all virtues — follow-through. BENNY JOHNSON RECALLS HOW CHARLIE KIRK HELPED HIS FAMILY AFTER ARSON DESTROYED THEIR DC HOME It was almost as if he could manifest things by sheer will. What’s been lost over the last year of well-deserved tributes and memorials to Charlie is just how unlikely his success truly was. The cauldron of suffering Charlie often endured was superhuman. He wanted to win back young people as an 18-year-old with zero money, zero connections and zero idea what he was doing, so he founded TPUSA. He wanted to be like his hero Rush Limbaugh and do a radio show, so he started The Charlie Kirk Show. He wanted the church to get off the sidelines and fight for America, so he launched TPUSA Faith. He wanted to build a grassroots army of ballot chasers to win elections, so he built Turning Point Action. But what’s been lost over the last year of well-deserved tributes and memorials to Charlie is just how unlikely his success truly was. The cauldron of suffering Charlie often endured was superhuman. BILL MAHER TO APPEAR IN CHARLIE KIRK DOCUMENTARY, REMEMBERS LOVING HIS INTERVIEW WITH THE TPUSA LEADER Charlie built TPUSA without taking a paycheck for the first five years. He lived off paltry speaking stipends and the generosity of friends who let him sleep on their couches. He served as the CEO, CMO, CFO and spokesman of TPUSA for years, spending over 300 days a year on the road, racking up enough frequent-flyer miles to reach top status on all the major airlines. When Charlie finally raised enough money to hire staff, he nearly missed payroll multiple times, working the phones or traveling through the night to break through with a donor who would support the "pipe dream" of turning young Americans into conservatives. The financial provision, which Charlie attributed to God’s faithfulness, always seemed to come through just in the nick of time. I was with Charlie when the years of cramped coach flights on his oversized frame finally took their toll on his back. One day, his body suddenly refused to move. I rushed him to the hospital, fearing something life-threatening, but the doctors determined he just needed to rest and stop the incessant travel. He, of course, refused. Although he sought out multiple fixes over the years, his back became a chronic thorn in his side. Many days on campus, he could barely walk up to the debate chair. Many of his most famous speeches were delivered through nearly unbearable pain. I’M A UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT. OUR PROFESSION SHOULD FINISH WHAT CHARLIE KIRK STARTED And, of course, there were the constant attacks. When I started working with Charlie, conservative media was awash in cheap hit pieces and op-eds attacking him and the organization. He was too abrasive, they said, too confrontational, too aggressive. They called him a charlatan, a grifter, and said TPUSA was all smoke and mirrors. Others would blame Charlie for Trump’s loss in 2020. Young voters went for Biden, and so that must be Charlie Kirk’s fault. Charlie was then thrown in front of the January 6 Committee to testify about an event he didn’t even attend. His COO, Tyler Bowyer, was prosecuted in the ridiculous alternative-electors witch hunt. And when Republican Kari Lake lost the governor’s race in Arizona in 2022 by a little more than 17,000 votes, Charlie was blamed again. SOCIALISM’S CAMPUS APPEAL MEETS GEN Z RESISTANCE AS STUDENTS KEEP SCORE ON COMMUNISM But each sling and each arrow only served to strengthen Charlie’s resolve to prove them all wrong. Charlie Kirk was the most remarkable man I’ve ever met. After Lake’s gubernatorial loss, Turning Point Action built out a tech and data platform custom-tailored to reach low-propensity voters. Chase the Vote, as it came to be called, blossomed into one of the most effective conservative voter-outreach machines ever built and transformed Arizona into the best-performing swing state in 2024. He did it all with boundless energy, decency, unflinching faith and a belief in the greatness of America. In short, he was the most remarkable man I’ve ever met. articles.title: Suvendu Adhikari's 'strict medicine' warning to 'anti-national' sympathisers at Jadavpur university
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Thursday warned that his government would take a tough approach towards those he described a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Thursday warned that his government would take a tough approach towards those he described as sympathisers of "anti-national forces" at Jadavpur University, saying they would need "strict medicines".Speaking in the state assembly, Adhikari said the government would respond in the language of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose rather than Mahatma Gandhi if slogans demanding freedom for Kashmir were raised on the university campus.He also said Jadavpur University would receive Rs 1,300 crore in grants, but warned that those raising slogans such as "Bharat tere tukde honge" would be dealt with firmly.CM backs university staff transfer BillAdhikari was speaking as the government introduced a Bill that would allow teaching and non-teaching employees to be transferred between state universities.The West Bengal Universities and Colleges (Administration and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was approved by the state Cabinet on September 8. It seeks to add a provision to Section 14A of the 2017 Act, allowing inter-university transfers of staff whenever required.Higher education minister Jagannath Chattopadhyay tabled the Bill during the special Assembly session. Adhikari described it as "important and necessary" and said its passage would be "historic".The government says the move will help newly established universities by allowing experienced teachers and other staff to be moved to institutions that need them. Adhikari said professors could help new universities develop infrastructure, improve teaching and work towards becoming centres of excellence.He said experienced teachers could be sent to institutions in places such as Jhargram and Cooch Behar, creating an exchange of human resources between universities.Teachers raise concerns over autonomyThe proposed changes have faced opposition from teachers' associations and academics, who fear that the government could interfere with university autonomy or selectively target teachers through transfers.Adhikari rejected such concerns and said the legislation would maintain a balance between institutional autonomy and accountability to the government."The Bill will balance institutes' autonomy and accountability towards the government... It would not impact PhD supervision and projects... Those unhappy with the provisions of the Bill are welcome to quit their jobs," he said.Explaining why the amendment was needed, Adhikari had earlier said, "This is important. There is a ground reality that necessitates the Bill."The chief minister also addressed the recent controversy surrounding a meat-related diktat by Dhirendra Shashtri of Bageshwar Dham. Referring to protests by Congress workers, he said he had instructed the Kolkata Police commissioner to arrest those who burnt portraits of the self-styled godman.Adhikari also referred to the 1970 murder of former Jadavpur University vice chancellor Gopal Sen. He said the government would set up a panel to investigate the incident if necessary.He further attributed the opposition's defeat in the West Bengal Assembly elections to what he called "disrespect" towards the saffron colour and claimed that the opposition would also lose the upcoming by-elections.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Global heat stuck on high: August was Earth’s hottest month on record, scientists say
articles.summary: Earth cooked to its hottest month on record in August, blowing far past a key climate threshold, due to human-caused climate change and a supersized El Nino.
articles.body: Earth cooked to its hottest month on record in August, blowing far past a key climate threshold, due to the dangerous double whammy of human-caused climate change and a supersized El Nino, according to the European climate service Copernicus. August’s sizzle also helped push the globe and the United States to swelter through the hottest Northern Hemisphere summer scientists have measured. Last month the world averaged 62.53 degrees Fahrenheit (16.96 degrees Celsius), which technically was one-hundredth of a degree Celsius more than the all-time global mark set in July 2023, but because that’s also the uncertainty level, it’s considered a tie, said Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for Copernicus. “It is now time to stop acting surprised that our warming planet keeps getting warmer. This is occurring exactly as forecast by scientists literally decades ago,” Texas A&M University climate scientist Andrew Dessler said in an email. “The interesting question is not whether we will keep breaking heat records (we will), but whether we’re going to do anything about it or just stand there while the climate train runs us over.” Globally, August was 1.65 degrees Celsius (nearly 3 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, far exceeding the longer term 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold set by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. The eight hottest months on record have all been from July 2023 on, according to Copernicus data. “Our climate system is really operating well outside the range we would have expected just a decade ago,” Burgess said Wednesday from a United Kingdom that has been beset with heat waves. “We’ve transitioned from climate being very abstract and perhaps impacting the global South or far away places to climate impacting and disrupting our daily lives with schools closing, hospitals being overwhelmed, roads melting, train lines buckling. And the reality is we will get more of these conditions that we’ve seen this summer.” Global monthly ocean temperatures in August tied a March 2024 all-time record for warmest month recorded, while Aug. 22 set a record for hottest day recorded in the world’s seas, according to Copernicus. An extra hot summer hits “This summer has really been exceptional. We’ve seen records that existed for close to 100 years be broken, in the U.S. in particular,” Burgess said. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration on Wednesday announced that for the first time, summer in the Lower 48 states was hotter than during the peak of the devastating Dust Bowl in 1936. June through August of 2026 in the contiguous United States averaged 74.37 degrees (23.54 degrees Celsius), nearly four tenths of a degree warmer than the mark set 90 years earlier. Globally, this past summer also tied, with 2024, for the hottest on record, according to Copernicus. In the U.S., August smashed heat records by more than half a degree Fahrenheit, averaging 75.58 degrees (24.21 degrees Celsius) and the average daytime high was a blistering 88.56 degrees (31.42 degrees Celsius), also a record. July was similarly record hot in the U.S., erasing another long-standing Dust Bowl mark. That records are regularly getting broken, and that August and not July which is traditionally warmer set an all-time record, are signs that human-caused climate change is accelerating, Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather said. Copernicus data goes back to 1940. NOAA data for the United States goes back to 1895 and global data, which generally matches Copernicus data but takes longer to calculate, dates back to 1880. Fossil fuels, El Nino blamed Several scientists said while El Nino is a factor, this natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps and warms weather globally is nowhere as big a cause as the heat-trapping gases emitted as humans burn coal, oil and natural gas. “While El Nino is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels. Climate change makes every El Nino hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London. Burgess said El Nino generally adds only one or two tenths of a degree Celsius (two to four tenths Fahrenheit) to the global temperature with the overwhelming rest of the heat coming from the burning of fossil fuels. This El Nino is forecast, however, to break records for strength in the coming months. And as temperatures continue to rise, heat waves, storms, floods and wildfires will get more frequent and more dangerous, said Texas Tech climate scientist Katharine Hayhoe. According to Hausfather, “it is increasingly likely that 2026 ends up beating 2024 as the warmest year on record, and almost certain that 2027 beats both, potentially reaching as high as 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels on the back of an unprecedentedly-strong El Nino event.” Some days may hit an even higher climate threshold, 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above mid 1800s, Burgess said. “Until humanity stops burning colossal amount of coal, oil and gas, the pollution this causes will keep baking our planet, and extreme heat will keep smashing all-time records, killing millions and costing trillions, hitting transport and health systems, and pushing up prices for household basics like food,” United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said. “This is the spiraling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fueling.”

articles.title: 'Treat Northeast people as Indians': Brother of Manipur musician beaten to death in Delhi
articles.summary: IMPHAL: The brother of Manipuri guitarist and music teacher Chongtham Vikram Singh urged the government to ensure that people from the Northeast are “.
articles.body: IMPHAL: The brother of Manipuri guitarist and music teacher Chongtham Vikram Singh urged the government to ensure that people from the Northeast are “properly treated as Indians” in the national capital.The statement came as the musician’s mortal remains arrived in Imphal following his death after an alleged assault in New Delhi.According to news agency ANI, Chongtham Vivek Singh said the family wanted justice for his brother and a safer environment for people from the Northeast.“We want justice and we want the government to ensure that people from the Northeast are properly treated as Indians in Delhi,” Vivek said.Vivek said the family hoped the authorities would take appropriate action and ensure that such incidents do not happen again.“It’s a very sad moment for us right now. The people of Manipur, and people from across the Northeast, have been suffering here in the capital of India, Delhi. This is a very painful and significant loss for all of us," Vivek added."We want justice- not only justice, but also an atmosphere in the capital of India where people coming from the Northeast are treated with dignity, respect, and equality. No one should have to face discrimination or feel unsafe simply because of where they come from, " Vivek further added.Singer Hamom Sadananda, who was present at the airport to receive Singh’s body, remembered him as a humble and down-to-earth person and called for strict action against those responsible for his death.“I am here to receive the dead body of my brother. He was a lovely, humble, and down-to-earth person. It is heartbreaking to see what has happened to him. It is extremely unfortunate that people from the Northeast continue to face discrimination in our own country," he said.He added, "Ye acha nhi ho rha hai…This is not right. We are citizens of India too, and we deserve to be treated with the same dignity, respect, and equality as every other citizen of this country. What has happened to my brother should never be repeated in India. I demand that the concerned authorities ensure justice and take the strictest possible action against those responsible, so that no one else has to suffer like this again.”The mortal remains of the 54-year-old musician arrived at Imphal International Airport on Wednesday, where grieving family members, friends, fellow musicians and local residents gathered to receive his body and demand justice over his death.Vikram Singh died in New Delhi following an alleged brutal assault in the Sunlight Colony, Kilokari village area.His death has triggered grief across Manipur and among the Manipuri community in Delhi. Family members and fellow musicians have also raised concerns over the safety, dignity and equal treatment of people from the Northeast in the national capital.The musician’s death has prompted mourning across the Northeast and among the community in Delhi.Hundreds of people gathered at Kangla Western Gate on Tuesday for a candlelight vigil in his memory.(With agency inputs)Stay updated with the latest Imphal news. articles.title: Twenty-five dead after fire erupts on cargo ship in Qingdao, eastern China - state media
articles.summary: Of the 42 people on board, 17 were were evacuated, CCTV reports.
articles.body:
Twenty-five people have been killed in a fire on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked at a port in eastern China, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.

Of the 42 people on board, 17 were were evacuated of which five are in hospital in stable condition, CCTV reports.

The vessel was undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in the city of Qingdao when the blaze erupted at around 11:15 local time (03:15 GMT). It was put out just over three hours later, according to CCTV.

Photos released by state media showed the vessel to be the Ocean Melody, a 190m (623ft) long Liberia-flagged carrier which arrived in Qingdao on 31 August, according to tracking site MarineTraffic.

Qingdao is a major trading hub and ranks among the world's busiest ports.

It is unclear what caused the fire. An eyewitness told the AFP news agency there was thick smoke rising from the ship, but he heard no explosion.

The country's leader Xi Jinping earlier called for "all-out" search and rescue efforts while Premier Li Qiang stressed the need to "prevent secondary disasters".

The fire comes nearly a month after a shipyard explosion in the south-eastern Chinese province of Fujian killed a rescue worker and injured 12 others.

articles.title: In 1969, an ornithologist began spending six months a year on a remote New York island; decades later, its tern colony had grown to more than 26,000 breeding pairs
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Helen Hays transformed Great Gull Island from an abandoned military site into one of North America's most significant seabird conservation areas, witnessing a tenfold increase in tern populations over 50 years.
articles.body: On a tiny island in Long Island Sound, an abandoned military outpost became home to one of North America’s most important seabird colonies. In 1969, ornithologist Helen Hays began spending roughly half of every year on Great Gull Island, living in former army buildings and working with volunteers to count, band and protect Common and Roseate Terns. More than five decades later, the island had become a major tern research and conservation site, with thousands of birds returning to breed each year.According to the American Museum of Natural History, Great Gull Island is a 17-acre former military outpost at the eastern end of Long Island Sound. The US Army occupied it as part of Fort Michie from 1897 to 1949, disrupting the island’s historic tern colony. After the fort was abandoned, the museum acquired the island in 1949 with the aim of restoring it as a breeding habitat for terns. The Linnaean Society of New York was tasked with preparing the island, removing parts of the abandoned military infrastructure and improving nesting areas. Terns returned in 1955, when 25 pairs of Common Terns were recorded, followed by Roseate Terns soon afterwards.From military outpost to tern sanctuaryAccording to the Linnaean Society of New York, the first clear sign that Great Gull Island could once again support a major tern colony came in 1955. Society member Irwin Alperin flew over the island and spotted 25 pairs of Common Terns nesting at its eastern end. Roseate Terns began nesting there soon afterwards. In 1963, Helen Hays visited the island with Catherine Pessino of the American Museum of Natural History and recognised its potential for long-term study of the two species. By 1969, Hays had recruited enough volunteers to spend the breeding season on the island and begin systematic monitoring of its tern populations.Conditions were far from comfortable for Hays and her team. The former military buildings were dilapidated, with leaky roofs, broken doors and windows, and cracked floors. Hays and her volunteers repaired what they could and converted the buildings into basic accommodation. She spent about six months on the island each year, from April to September, before returning to Manhattan for the rest of the year. Her work combined conservation with intensive field research. Volunteers banded chicks and captured adults for identification, allowing researchers to follow individual birds when they returned in subsequent years. The long-running programme generated information on population changes, nesting behaviour and habitat conditions, while bringing together volunteers, students and scientists.A growing colony and a scientific recordThe Linnaean Society of New York records a striking increase in the island’s tern population over the decades. At the beginning of the long-term project, Great Gull Island supported approximately 3,000 breeding pairs of Common and Roseate Terns. By 2014, more than 26,000 nesting pairs of Common Terns had been recorded on the island. Maintaining suitable nesting habitat required active management because the two species use the island differently. Common Terns favour open nesting areas, while Roseate Terns tend to select more sheltered locations, including spaces beneath rocks and specially provided nest structures. Vegetation can also make areas unsuitable for Common Terns, which prefer relatively open ground. Habitat management therefore became an important part of maintaining suitable breeding conditions, including the use of meadow voles to help control vegetation.The island’s long-term research has also documented environmental threats to the birds. According to the US Geological Survey, three Roseate Tern chicks found with congenital abnormalities at Great Gull Island in 1970 contained high levels of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and DDE, raising concerns about the effects of persistent chemical pollutants on the species. A later 1981 survey examined organochlorine residues in Roseate Tern eggs from major colonies and investigated whether contamination was associated with changes in eggshell characteristics.The combination of habitat management, long-term monitoring and research has given Great Gull Island an importance far beyond its small size. The Linnaean Society of New York describes it as supporting the world’s largest nesting colony of Common Terns and the largest Roseate Tern colony in the Western Hemisphere, making the former military outpost an important site for understanding and protecting these seabirds.A legacy built one summer at a timeThe island is small, but its importance extends far beyond its 17 acres. Its isolation and protected nesting habitat have helped make it suitable for large colonies of seabirds, while decades of monitoring have created a valuable record linking individual birds with their breeding sites and movements. Hays eventually ended her annual summer stays after spending roughly half a century working on the island. The programme she established, however, continued through the Linnaean Society of New York, volunteers and researchers.The American Museum of Natural History has also preserved materials from the project, including field notes and other documents, helping maintain a record of the long-running work. What began in 1969 with Hays and volunteers living for months in deteriorating former army buildings developed into one of the longest-running tern research programmes in the region. Great Gull Island remains both a protected breeding site and an important location for studying Common and Roseate Terns, including their population trends, breeding behaviour and movements.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2021, Singapore tested heat-reflecting coatings on roads, roofs and walls; a field study found afternoon air up to 3.6°F cooler and thermal comfort improved by 2.7°F
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Singapore's innovative use of heat-reflective coatings on roads and buildings significantly cools urban temperatures, improving pedestrian comfort as part of a groundbreaking field study.
articles.body: The specific type of heat that rises off concrete and asphalt long after the sun has set is familiar to anyone who has strolled through a tropical metropolis in the middle of the afternoon. This phenomenon is known to scientists as the "urban heat island effect." Due to its near-equator location and year-round warmth, Singapore has more incentive than other cities to take that effect seriously. As a result, researchers there opted to test a solution that had, until then, mostly existed in labs and computer models.A team from Nanyang Technological University worked with a JTC Corporation-managed industrial estate in the west of the island to apply specially formulated cool paint and additives meant to reflect a greater portion of incoming sunlight rather than absorb it as heat to the roofs, walls, and road pavement of a portion of the site. Researchers were able to directly compare the two surroundings under identical weather conditions over a prolonged monitoring period by using a nearby, uncoated portion of similar buildings and street layout as the control.Turning two industrial streets into a live experimentWhat set this study apart from earlier research was its scale and setting. According to NTU Singapore, most prior studies of cool paint coatings had relied on computer simulations or small, scaled-down models, leaving a real gap in understanding of how the approach performs in an actual tropical street. The NTU team picked four rectangular buildings that formed two parallel street canyons and small corridors with buildings on either side. They applied the reflective coating to one canyon while leaving the other unpainted as a control. During the study, environmental sensors measured air movement, surface and air temperature, humidity and radiation at both sites, providing a complete picture of how the coating affected circumstances hour by hour.The results, later published in the journal Sustainable Cities and Society, showed that the coated canyon released up to thirty per cent less heat from its surfaces across a full day and night cycle. That reduction meant air temperatures in the covered canyon were up to two degrees Celsius, or about 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, colder than in the uncoated canyon during the hottest period of the afternoon, usually around 4 o'clock. Pedestrian thermal comfort, assessed with an international benchmark called the Universal Thermal Climate Index, improved by up to 1.5 degrees Celsius, or around 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, in the treated region.What really made a difference on the groundThe way the coating works is relatively straightforward. The research team said the cool-paint-covered roofs reflected about 50 per cent more sunlight and absorbed up to 40 per cent less heat at the hottest point of the day compared to the untreated roofs, while the painted walls kept much of the solar energy from entering the buildings in the first place. With less heat stored during the day, less heat was radiated back into the street canyon after sunset. “The findings are significant enough to be able to warrant a wider use of cool coatings on built-up surfaces, on a bigger scale,” said Assistant Professor Ng Bing Feng from NTU’s School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, one of the study’s co-authors. Singapore's authorities have moved to expand the approach beyond the original test site, with JTC piloting reflective paint coatings at industrial parks in other parts of the island, a development NTU's Energy Research Institute has tracked as the research moves toward wider application.Why a coat of paint could matter to cities far beyond SingaporeOne of the attractive features of cool paint coatings is the relatively low disturbance they require compared to other thermal mitigation methods. It will take years to get real cooling from planting mature trees or rebuilding entire streetscapes, but a coating can be applied relatively quickly to existing roofs, walls and pavements at a fraction of the cost of major reconstruction. The Singapore findings give a rare example of a little intrusive solution with an immediate, independently measured effect for densely built, heat-stressed cities across South and Southeast Asia, where land is scarce and adding green cover is often challenging. As more governments seek out pragmatic ways to reduce temperatures at the street level without waiting decades for trees to grow, a fresh layer of reflective paint could prove to be one of the more quietly effective tools in the kit.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Girl Scout Cookies going to the dogs as vet warns against 'unintentionally overfeeding'
articles.summary: A veterinarian weighs in on the Girl Scouts' first-ever dog cookie, sharing why pet owners should limit treats to 10% of their dog's daily diet.
articles.body: Girl Scout Cookie season is going to the dogs. For the first time, Girl Scouts of the USA will offer a cookie made specifically for dogs when the 2027 cookie season kicks off. The new Patch Pals are soft-baked, blueberry muffin-flavored dog treats created in collaboration with BARK, the company behind BarkBox. DOG TREAT FOUNDER EATS HER OWN PRODUCTS, EVEN PACKS THEM IN HER KIDS' LUNCHES "Each dog cookie has been baked to feature one of four 'patch' designs, representing iconic Girl Scout experiences," Girl Scouts of the USA said in a news release. Ben Donati, an emergency veterinarian at Apex Vets in Silver Spring, Maryland, said his first reaction to the unusual addition was excitement — followed by surprise that it hadn't happened sooner. The treats make sense, Donati told Fox News Digital, as Americans increasingly consider their pets part of the family. "So, probably a light bulb went off in someone's mind that, why not sell to the four-legged member of the family," he said. But while man's best friend can now get in on the Girl Scout Cookie tradition, Donati cautioned owners against letting their dogs overindulge. GORDON RAMSAY RESPONDS TO 'OVEREXAGGERATED' REACTION AFTER ALLEGED DOG-INSIDE-RESTAURANT DRAMA "We tend to say about 10% of their diet should come from treats, or up to 10% really," Donati said. Nothing about the Patch Pals ingredients jumped out at Donati as "super alarming," though he said treats are not a substitute for a complete and balanced diet. "Probably shouldn't eat a whole box of Girl Scout Cookies," he said. "Probably shouldn't eat a whole box of Patch Pals." The new product also comes as Americans' relationships with their pets have become increasingly human-like. "There is an emotional component to it. There's a psychological component to it," Donati said. "We anthropomorphize our pets. We take pictures of them where they look like they're smiling." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER That affection, however, can translate into extra calories. Donati said overweight dogs tend to have shorter lifespans than their leaner counterparts, while excess weight can also put additional strain on their joints. He said one of the most common mistakes owners make with treats is "unintentionally overfeeding them." Owners of food-motivated dogs can consider using some of the animal's normal kibble allotment as rewards during walks or training rather than continually adding extra treats, Donati said. Treats can have behavioral consequences, too. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "It's just getting the behavior that you reward," Donati said, noting that owners can inadvertently reinforce unwanted behaviors by offering a treat at the wrong moment. Still, Donati gave the Girl Scouts' canine cookie experiment an enthusiastic reception. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Overall, I think it's great," he said, adding that the treats should "add a lot of fun for the girls who are selling them and the families who are buying them." articles.title: Charlie Kirk assassination: New UVU president says it will continue to 'host the frays,' embrace free speech
articles.summary: UVU's new president revealed his two daughters were just yards from Charlie Kirk's assassination and vowed to continue fostering free speech on campus.
articles.body: PROVO, Utah — A year after Charlie Kirk was assassinated in the central courtyard at Utah Valley University, school officials will close campus for the day — as the school's new president revealed his own daughters were at the scene and vowed to continue to foster free speech in higher education. Dr. Jon Anderson, who joined UVU just before the start of the fall 2026 semester, was in his prior role as president of Pennsylvania Western University when Kirk was shot and killed on Sept. 10, 2025, but his family has roots in Utah, he told Fox News Digital in a sitdown interview. His wife called him to break the news, he said. JUDGE IN ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S CASE EXPLAINS WHY DEATH PENALTY REMAINS ON TABLE IN WRITTEN ORDER "I had two daughters and a son-in-law. They were about 10 yards from the assassination when it happened," he said. "And so I knew that our future would be tied to it in one way or the other." The healing process: "When the opportunity came up to come home — this is the place that I'm from — and help this institution move forward and heal, it's something I leaned into immediately," he told Fox News Digital. "I wanted to be here to help in any way that I could, and I have found since coming here, this place is so resilient. Its people are gritty, they're ready to move forward, and they're to learn from everything that we can learn from that day." ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY With students, faculty and other campus staff dealing with Kirk's assassination in their own ways, Anderson said the campus will be closed on Sept. 10, the one-year mark. "I think one thing all of us at UVU have learned is that traumatic events, sometimes there's an initial reaction and sometimes there is a delayed reaction, and it's important for us to be very empathetic with each other as everyone goes through the healing process in their own way," he added. ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION Although the school is not hosting an official event, he said Turning Point USA plans to hold its own memorial on campus. "We want people to have their own space to heal in their own way," he said. "TPUSA is using some space on campus to hold their event here, and we are supportive and reflective of that." HOW CHARLIE KIRK INSPIRED HIS MENTOR'S FIGHT TO DEFEND REALITY Kirk was a founder of TPUSA and was speaking at an event sponsored by its UVU chapter at the heart of campus when he was killed. The group will hold its memorial at UVU's UCCU Center at 6:30 p.m. MT on Sept. 10. As for plans for a potential permanent memorial, Anderson said work is underway from a group including board members and students. "They're sorting through lots of voices, getting people to the table to talk through what that might look like, looking at other institutions, what they have done," he said. "I can't guarantee that it's going to be anytime soon, but I can tell you if and when that happens, it will be thoughtfully done and well placed." INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES On free speech: While the public university is "politically neutral and apolitical," Anderson said it's important to provide a space to share varied viewpoints for the students' benefit. "We allow people to come in and focus on civil dialogue, engaging in new and good ideas, and that's where we hope to excel," he continued. articles.title: Satya Niketan building collapse: Can a 'no-responsibility' clause shield a PG owner?
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Satya Niketan building collapse, which killed seven people and injured several others, has raised questions about who can be held respo.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Satya Niketan building collapse, which killed seven people and injured several others, has raised questions about who can be held responsible when people living in private paying guest (PG) accommodation are exposed to an unsafe building. The issue has gained a legal dimension after the rent agreement signed by residents of the PG reportedly contained clauses limiting the hostel's responsibility for casualties, injuries and loss or damage in certain circumstances.The incident has also prompted the Delhi high court to examine whether responsibility for the tragedy, if negligence is established, could extend beyond the building owner. While hearing a PIL, the court questioned the role of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) and Delhi University (DU), and noted that inadequate hostel accommodation leaves many outstation students dependent on private PG facilities.This raises a larger question: can an owner avoid liability for a death or injury simply because residents signed an agreement containing a clause saying the PG was not responsible for casualties?Can a PG owner escape liability through a ‘no-responsibility’ clause?The agreement signed by residents of the Hostel Daze PG contained provisions limiting the establishment's responsibility for casualties and for personal injury or loss or damage to belongings in certain situations, including events described as being beyond the control of the PG.But such a clause does not by itself settle the question of legal responsibility, said Vivek Narayan Sharma, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of India.Sharma said a private agreement can decide who bears certain lawful risks, but it cannot be used to permit conduct that violates a legal duty.“A false disclaimer cannot be a licence to delay or breach the law. Real hazards outside of one's influence can be agreed upon, but not legal safety measures or liability for personal misconduct,” Sharma said.He referred to Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which deals with agreements that have an unlawful object or are opposed to public policy.“An agreement can apportion lawful risks. It cannot legitimise an unlawful risk,” Sharma said.In simple terms, a tenant may agree that the owner will not be responsible for an unexpected event genuinely outside the owner's control. That is different from using the same clause to escape responsibility for an unsafe building or harm caused by the owner's own conduct.What if the collapse was linked to negligent maintenance or unsafe construction?The legal position would depend heavily on what caused the collapse and whether the owner or someone acting on the owner's behalf was responsible for the dangerous condition.Sharma said that if negligent maintenance, an unsafe structure or unauthorised construction, renovation or alteration caused or materially contributed to the collapse, the case would have to be examined on the basis of the owner's legal duty, whether that duty was breached, whether the breach caused the incident and what damage resulted.“No disclaimer can get rid of duty. Should the defendant's negligent maintenance, unsafe structure, and/or unauthorised renovation or alteration have caused or materially contributed to the event, liability might turn on the issues of duty, breach, causation and damage rather than an exclusion clause,” he said.This would also affect clauses dealing with events described in the agreement as being beyond the owner's control.“Coverage for events ‘beyond the owner’s control’ is usually not available if they result from the owner’s own conduct,” Sharma said.Therefore, the exact cause of the collapse would be central. A contractual clause dealing with an unforeseen event outside the owner's control would raise a different question from one being relied upon after an accident allegedly linked to unsafe construction or negligent work.Does signing the agreement mean residents accepted the risk?Sharma said residents cannot normally be treated as having accepted the risk of living in an unsafe building simply because they signed the agreement.A resident may accept ordinary and disclosed risks associated with living in a rented property. But that does not mean the person has given up the right to expect the premises to be structurally safe and legally compliant.“A resident may consent to normal, revealed risks, but generally cannot be regarded as having relinquished the right to a structurally safe and lawfully compliant dwelling,” Sharma said.He said the issue becomes more serious where a risk is concealed or involves an illegal alteration or other unsafe condition known to the owner.“Freedom of contract has its footing in the law, not above it,” Sharma said.Can families of those killed still seek compensation?The disclaimer would not automatically prevent the families of those killed or injured from seeking compensation, Sharma said.“Once negligence and causation are proven, a private disclaimer cannot, by itself, negate the remedies of the family,” he said.Depending on the circumstances, families could pursue relevant civil, public or consumer-law remedies. The exact route would depend on the facts and the evidence available.The existence of the disclaimer may be considered during the proceedings, but it would not automatically defeat a claim based on actionable negligence.“The presence of the disclaimer may be taken into account but it cannot automatically cut off a claim based on actionable negligence,” Sharma said.Can the agreement protect the owner from criminal liability?A private contract cannot waive criminal liability, Sharma said.“No. Criminal liability cannot be waived,” he said.If an investigation establishes that a person's death was caused by a rash or negligent act and the statutory requirements are met, Section 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, could become relevant.The prosecution would still have to prove the required elements, including the rash or negligent conduct and its proximate connection with the death. The existence of a disclaimer would not prevent an investigation or prosecution.“The prosecution shall have to prove the rash or negligent act behavior, coupled with the death, as a proximate correlative. An agreement entered into between private individuals can’t give immunity in future,” Sharma said.Could MCD also face liability?The high court's questions have widened the issue beyond the private agreement between the PG and its residents. Sharma said MCD's liability would depend on what the civic body knew about the building, what legal duties it had and whether it failed to act despite being aware of a possible danger.“If MCD had complaints, notices, inspection reports, or it had knowledge of violations and it negligently failed to take action, then some liability in the public authority may be contributed to, depending upon the evidence as to duty, breach and causation,” he said.This would not mean MCD is automatically responsible because the building was within its jurisdiction. Evidence would be needed to establish a legal duty, a failure to perform that duty and a connection between that failure and the deaths or injuries.The tragedy has also led to calls for closer scrutiny of buildings and action against unauthorised construction. The Indian Chamber of Construction Industry (ICCI), expressing grief over the Satya Niketan incident, appealed to authorities to evaluate such structures and prohibit unauthorised and unapproved construction, which it described as a potential hazard.Could Delhi University be held responsible because students depended on private PGs?Sharma said DU's position would be different from that of the building owner or a civic authority responsible for enforcing building rules.The high court had noted that limited hostel accommodation leaves students, particularly those coming from outside Delhi, dependent on private PG accommodation. But that circumstance alone would not make the university legally responsible for what happens inside a privately operated building.“Delhi University is not the same. Students being forced to stay in private PGs due to lack of hostel accommodation does not automatically give rise to legal liability,” Sharma said.For DU to face liability, there would have to be a specific legal duty that it was required to perform, evidence that the duty was breached and a causal link between that breach and the harm.“There must be a specific legal duty which has been breached as well as a causal link to the injury,” he said.Thus, the shortage of university accommodation may explain why students turn to private PGs, but it is legally different from establishing that the university caused or contributed to the collapse.Who could ultimately be held responsible for the tragedy?Sharma said responsibility may not necessarily fall on only one party. The final assessment would depend on who created the risk, who knew about it, who was legally required to address it and whose conduct contributed to the tragedy.“In the end, the liabilities would be concurrent among everything and hinge upon who engendered that risk, who became conscious of it, who had been legally liable to counteract the hazard, and whose negligent conduct led to the unfriendly event,” Sharma said.This means the owner, contractor, civic authorities or other parties could have different levels of responsibility depending on the evidence. The rent agreement alone would not determine that questionSharma summed up the distinction between private contracts and legal safety duties:“A private owner cannot by contract avoid a duty to make sure a building is safe; a public authority cannot hide from a known dangerous building with an administrative dismissal. If both sides are negligent in bringing about the same tragedy, liability need not end at one door,” he said.Ultimately, the Satya Niketan case will turn on the investigation into the building's condition, the circumstances surrounding the repair or alteration work, what the different authorities knew or were required to do, and whether any act or omission can be linked to the deaths and injuries.

articles.title: SC seeks UP govt response on plea challenging MLAs, MLCs’ pension, perks
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday sought responses from the Uttar Pradesh government and others on a plea challenging provisions of a 1980 law .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday sought responses from the Uttar Pradesh government and others on a plea challenging provisions of a 1980 law that provide pension and other facilities to sitting and former MLAs and MLCs in the state.A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta issued notice on the petition challenging a May verdict of the Lucknow bench of the Allahabad High Court, which had dismissed the plea against the constitutional validity of the provisions.The top court posted the matter for hearing after four weeks.Plea questions benefits to legislatorsThe petitioner, Lok Prahari, had challenged provisions of the Uttar Pradesh State Legislature (Members' Emoluments and Pension) Act, 1980, arguing that the state legislature had effectively made itself the “judge in its own cause” by granting benefits to its sitting and former members.The plea contended that the benefits were “manifestly arbitrary” and contrary to the constitutional principle that public office is meant for public service and not personal gain.The High Court had noted that the law provides sitting and former MLAs and MLCs with salary, allowances and other facilities. It also extends pension, family pension, free travel, medical facilities and other amenities to their spouses, family members and companions.What petitioner arguedThe petitioner contended that these provisions go beyond the powers conferred on state legislatures under Article 195 of the Constitution.Article 195 deals with the salaries and allowances of members of state Legislative Assemblies and Legislative Councils. According to the petitioner, it does not specifically provide for pension, post-retirement benefits or facilities for family members and companions.What Allahabad HC saidThe High Court, however, had held that the challenge was essentially based on a policy disagreement rather than any demonstrable constitutional infirmity.It observed that the constitutional scheme does not prevent a legislature from making provisions for pension, allowances or allied benefits for its members, including former members.While dismissing the plea, the High Court had said there was no constitutional bar on the state legislature enacting measures of social security for its current and former members.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Could kill us all': Another AI employee quits, sounds alarm over safety
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Another AI employee has quit over safety concerns, adding to a growing list of researchers and employees who have publicly warned that the race to dev.
articles.body: Another AI employee has quit over safety concerns, adding to a growing list of researchers and employees who have publicly warned that the race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems is moving too fast.Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who spent the past three years conducting pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, announced his resignation from Anthropic in a post on X. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote, accusing both companies of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon said. He warned that future AI systems could become capable of hacking systems, transforming entire fields and acquiring real-world power and resources.Coxon is the latest AI worker to publicly raise concerns about the technology’s development. Several employees at major AI companies have quit or spoken out over fears that advances in AI could outpace efforts to keep the systems under human control.In July, nearly 1,400 AI company employees signed an open letter calling for stronger regulation and a slower pace of development to improve AI safety, according to a CNN report.Coxon said that while the risks are understood at Anthropic, the company remains caught in a race with other AI developers. “Accepting this race and entering the ‘endgame’ is a hubristic gamble that should not be launched from a private company’s Slack,” he said.He called for greater coordination between AI companies and governments and said a temporary ban on improving model capabilities could be among the measures needed to prevent a global race.His comments were backed by Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger, who wrote: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger later said he personally puts the chance of this happening over the next decade at under 10%.Anthropic said it has “always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks” and that it continues to build models with strong safeguards.The latest resignation comes as AI leaders themselves acknowledge growing safety concerns. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki recently warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than researchers’ ability to reliably monitor and control them.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Drax ash mound extraction plan approved for Selby site
articles.summary: Plans to extract and reuse million tonnes of ash from a mound next to Drax are given the go-ahead.
articles.body:
Plans to extract up to 23.5 million tonnes of ash from a disposal site next to Drax Power Station have been approved.

The 161-hectare (398 acre) mound, immediately north-west of the power station near Selby, reaches up to 39 metres (128ft) and has been used for ash deposits from Drax since the 1970s.

The scheme would see ash recovered for use in construction products such as concrete, reducing the need for virgin aggregates, with extraction continuing until 2045 and restoration completed by 2055.

Although North Yorkshire Council approved the application by Drax Power Ltd, it imposed conditions on when the site could be worked following concerns from residents.

Objections from three people cited concerns about dust, noise, lighting, air pollution and the impact on the landscape.

Concerns were also raised about habitat loss, the scale and duration of the scheme, and the removal of screening that helps shield Drax Power Station from nearby communities, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

Councillor Tim Thrall, from Barlow Parish Council, who spoke at the planning meeting, said in principle they had "no objection to the removal of the ash mound."

He added: "However, we do have a number of concerns about whether mitigation measures are enough to impact the quality of life of the residents of the village."

Another councillor Mark Crane, whose area includes Barlow, said proposals that the site was to operate 18 hours a day, from 06:00 until midnight, seven days a week excluding bank holidays, "blew his mind".

He added: "To expect them to accept that they can work from six in the morning till midnight every single day of the year is, I'm sorry, completely unreasonable."

The planning committee agreed the site could only be worked from 08:00 until 20:00, excluding Sundays and bank holidays.

The committee also agreed a condition to ensure that 65% of the ash was transported by rail with the remainder removed by road.

Council officers concluded that, subject to conditions, the development would not result in unacceptable impacts on residents, highways, ecology, air quality or the water environment.

The approval was also subject to a legal agreement that includes a £200,000 fund to help mitigate its impact on the surrounding landscape.

articles.title: How 9/11 transformed synagogue security into a new reality for the Jewish community
articles.summary: FBI data shows Jews face 63% of religiously motivated hate crimes as communities prepare for Rosh Hashanah on Friday, Sept. 11 amid rising threats.
articles.body: At sundown on Friday, Sept. 11, as America marks 25 years since the terrorist attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people, Jewish families across the country will welcome in Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish new year marking 5787. They will enter synagogues at the moment of peak annual attendance, walking past armed guards, security cameras, secured doors and bag checks. The convergence brings into focus how the Sept. 11 attacks transformed security in American synagogues and helped create the national infrastructure that now protects Jewish life. FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE When Rosh Hashanah began six days after the attacks in 2001, a security guard stationed outside a synagogue was still unusual. Twenty-five years later, security is no longer an occasional precaution. It has become a permanent precondition of Jewish communal life. "The confluence of events, the 25th anniversary of 9/11 and Rosh Hashanah, is really very meaningful to us," Eric Fingerhut, president and CEO of Jewish Federations of North America, told Fox News Digital. "If you trace the evolution of the security situation for the Jewish community in North America, you see that 9/11 really was a major turning point." Before the attacks, Fingerhut said, synagogues may have relied on police to direct traffic during the High Holidays or installed basic alarm systems, but there was no widespread belief that Jewish communities needed protection from threats to their physical safety. "That changed on 9/11," he said. "The Jewish community understood quite clearly that the people who attacked the World Trade Center and the Pentagon were attacking America that day, but they had a special animus for the Jewish community and the Jewish people." Fingerhut said that shift led Jewish Federations of North America to help create the Secure Community Network after 9/11, giving communities a model for protecting Jewish institutions and a unified channel to federal law enforcement. For generations, Rosh Hashanah preparation meant apples and honey, prayer books and the shofar. Now the checklist also includes secured entrances, emergency plans and congregants standing watch while their neighbors pray. The price of that new reality is staggering. MARYLAND SYNAGOGUE SUES COUNTY OVER LAW RESTRICTING CONCEALED CARRY NEAR HOUSES OF WORSHIP A national study by Jewish Federations of North America found that Jewish communal institutions spend an estimated $1 billion annually on security. Based on an examination of more than 4,500 institutions, that amounts to nearly $2.8 million every day simply to keep Jewish life open and accessible. The organization leads the national initiative placing professional security directors across all 141 Federation communities. Rabbi Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, described the contrast on his own block. "If you walk past the churches on our block, the doors are wide open, inviting people in," Steinmetz told Fox News Digital. "But at our synagogue, there are security cameras, a double door system and a line of guards outside, at the cost of untold thousands of dollars." That security is no longer reserved for major institutions or large cities. From New York and Florida to Michigan and Los Angeles, ordinary worshipers are training in situational awareness, access control, surveillance detection, emergency response and coordination with law enforcement. The Community Security Service, or CSS, said more than 20,000 people completed its training in 2025. Of those, 6,100 volunteers protected 440 synagogues and nearly 100 Jewish events, logging more than 300,000 guard hours across 24 states. The Secure Community Network (SCN) provides national intelligence and coordination. In 2025, it recorded 4,400 incident reports, trained 40,000 people and made 851 referrals to law enforcement. "While the threat environment accelerates, our community has never been more prepared, informed or engaged," Michael Masters, SCN’s national director and CEO, told Fox News Digital. "This year our Duty Desk logged nearly 3,200 threat incidents, pacing ahead of last year." Steinmetz said threats to the Jewish community "exploded after Oct. 7th," adding that "the hatred of Israel encourages antisemites to come out of the woodwork." The FBI recorded 1,528 hate crime incidents targeting Jews in 2025, representing 63% of the nation’s 2,408 religiously motivated incidents. Jews comprise roughly 2% of the U.S. population, yet incidents targeting Jews represented 14% of all hate crimes reported nationwide. ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE ESCALATES AS DEADLY WEAPON ATTACKS SURGE IN 2025: REPORT During the first eight months of 2026, major crime fell 6.2% across New York City, while confirmed hate crimes targeting Jews rose 8%, from 212 to 229, according to new NYPD figures. That averages nearly one such crime every 25 hours. Fox News Digital contacted NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch about the department’s High Holiday preparations. The NYPD said it will hold a briefing ahead of the holidays and provide additional security details at that time. In neighboring New Jersey, the state Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness (NJOHSP) said it is coordinating with the state Attorney General’s Office, New Jersey State Police, the FBI’s Newark field office, local law enforcement and community partners. "Together, we are protecting houses of worship, helping ensure every New Jerseyan can practice their faith without fear, and keeping New Jersey safe and secure," NJOHSP said. The coordination follows recent attacks on Jewish institutions. On Aug. 14, a man was charged with allegedly disrupting a Friday night service attended by approximately 375 people at Manhattan’s Central Synagogue, damaging ceremonial candlesticks and assaulting a congregant and security guard. The charges against include federal hate crimes and damaging religious property resulting in bodily injury. Five months earlier, an attacker inspired by Hezbollah rammed a pickup truck carrying gasoline and fireworks through the doors of Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan, according to the FBI. Armed with a rifle and hundreds of rounds, he struck one security guard and exchanged gunfire with others. Inside were 140 children at the synagogue’s early childhood center. Every child and staff member escaped without physical injury and the guard survived. For Steven Ingber, CEO of the Jewish Federation of Detroit, the assault remains a powerful reminder of the need for vigilance as families prepare to gather. "We take the security of our community with the utmost seriousness, and, of course, the assault on Temple Israel remains fresh in our minds," Ingber said. "We will enter the High Holidays vigilant and prepared. But we will also enter them with confidence and pride." Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in suburban Detroit, who also serves as president of the Michigan Board of Rabbis, said Jewish Michiganders are entering the new year "with a feeling of heaviness." "From marking the 25th year since the terrorist attacks on 9/11 to marking six months since the terrorist attack on our community and especially our children, anxieties are heightened," Starr told Fox News Digital exclusively. "We enter with heaviness, but we are also filled with hope for a better tomorrow." LOX & LOADED: JEWISH GUN GROUP PARTNERS WITH NRA AMID RISING ANTISEMITISM "No family should have to weigh their safety against their faith," Fingerhut said. Employing one full-time security guard costs an estimated $90,000 annually, according to Jewish Federations of North America. The organization is advocating for greater federal support through the bipartisan Jewish American Security Act, which would strengthen security assistance for at-risk nonprofit institutions. For Jewish communities, the question is no longer whether security is necessary, but who will bear the growing cost of making worship possible. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Steinmetz called that cost "a vicious tax on the Jewish community," one "levied by the antisemites." For Fingerhut, the purpose of security is not simply to prevent an attack. It is to ensure fear never determines whether a Jewish family participates in Jewish life. "We do not want anyone to make the choice not to participate in Jewish life because they are afraid for their safety," Fingerhut said. "What we have learned is that the visible presence of security, and the real impact of that security, is what enables and encourages people to come out and participate in Jewish life." Fingerhut’s message to Jewish communities in America and around the world was clear: do not retreat, but continue to "lean into Jewish life." He said, "We will make sure that there is safety and security in place so that we can all feel confident in our involvement in Jewish life." articles.title: IRCTC scam case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against Lalu, Rabri Devi and Tejashwi
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court on Thursday ordered the framing of charges against former railway minister Lalu Prasad Yadav and others in the alleged IRCTC .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Delhi court on Thursday ordered the framing of charges against former railway minister Lalu Prasad Yadav and others in the alleged IRCTC hotels money laundering case, observing that there was a strong suspicion of abuse of office during his tenure.The court said railway officials manipulated the tender process under Prasad’s stewardship to facilitate the award of leases for IRCTC-run hotels in Ranchi and Pune. It also said the nature, timing and course of the investigation in the case were not inspired by political vendetta, reported PTI.The court also ordered framing of charges against former Bihar chief minister Rabri Devi, her son Tejashwi Yadav, Lara Projects, Sujata Hotels and four others. The charges include corruption, criminal conspiracy and cheating against Lalu Prasad, while Rabri Devi and Tejashwi face conspiracy and cheating charges.The case stems from alleged irregularities in the award of contracts to operate two IRCTC hotels. The CBI has alleged that the tender process was manipulated and conditions were tweaked to favour Sujata Hotels during Lalu Prasad's tenure as railway minister. The ED has alleged that the transactions were part of a larger money-laundering conspiracy.The accused have pleaded not guilty and the case will now proceed to trial. The framing of charges and the court's observations at this stage do not amount to a finding of guilt.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Karnataka government on Thursday directed that the national song ‘Vande Mataram’ be played or sung at all state government programmes and official ceremonies.According to a government order dated September 8, 2026, the decision was taken in accordance with guidelines issued by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs.The order states that, except at programmes attended by the President, Vice President, Prime Minister or Governor, only the first two stanzas of ‘Vande Mataram’ shall be sung at all state government programmes.
