articles.title: In the 1820s, giant reed reached California for erosion control; two centuries later it crowds out native plants and has doubled or tripled wildfire fuel in parts of Southern California
articles.summary: US News: A plant brought to California nearly 200 years ago has become a serious invasive weed in parts of the state. Giant reed, also known as arundo, was fir.
articles.body: A plant brought to California nearly 200 years ago has become a serious invasive weed in parts of the state. Giant reed, also known as arundo, was first planted in California in the 1820s to provide roofing material and help control erosion in the Los Angeles Basin.According to Center for invasive species research, the plant, scientifically known as Arundo donax, is native to eastern Asia. It was widely planted in different parts of the world because it could be used for several purposes, including walking sticks, fishing poles and musical instruments. It is also being investigated as a possible biofuel source.Over time, however, giant reed became an invasive weed in several regions where it was introduced. The University of California, Riverside’s Center for Invasive Species Research lists California among the areas where the plant has become a problem, along with parts of Texas, Hawaii, Nevada, Utah, Missouri, Virginia, New Mexico and Florida.One reason giant reed can spread so effectively is its rapid growth. The plant can grow about 4 inches a day and reach a mature height of 25 feet in about 12 months. It can also tolerate a range of environmental conditions, allowing it to grow in damp riparian areas and in moderately saline soils.Dense growth pushes out native plantsGiant reed can form dense stands that leave little room for native vegetation. Native plants are typically displaced when arundo becomes established. Animals associated with those native plants may also be unable to use the dense stands of giant reed, leading to declines in their populations.The problem is particularly serious in California, where arundo can choke out native willows. Its presence also creates a fire risk because the plant can provide large amounts of fuel in riparian areas, where fires are typically uncommon.The plant is also well adapted to fire. This creates another problem because fires can help promote arundo invasions in sensitive habitats. In the Santa Ana River Basin in Southern California, the fire fuel load in riparian areas has almost tripled because of arundo infestations.The plant can create problems during floods as well. Large amounts of arundo can be dislodged and carried by floodwater. These pieces can form large rafts, and tons of the plant can build up around bridge supports. Such accumulations can cause bridges to collapse.Giant reed also uses large amounts of waterThe invasive plant's impact is not limited to native vegetation and fire risk. Its water use has also been studied in the Santa Ana River.Research cited by the Center for Invasive Species Research estimated that arundo transpires 56,200 acre-feet of water each year on the Santa Ana River. Native vegetation was estimated to consume 18,700 acre-feet.The difference was estimated at 37,500 acre-feet of water. The study said that if arundo were not drawing this water from the Santa Ana River Basin, there would be enough water to serve a population of about 190,000 people.The same study estimated that purchasing that amount of untreated water from the Metropolitan Water Association would have cost approximately $12 million in 1993 dollars. The economic study was conducted in 1993.Scientists studying ways to control itResearchers at the University of California are studying the invasion ecology of arundo and different ways to control it. These include the use of herbicides and mechanical removal from areas where the plant has spread.Another approach being developed by USDA-ARS researchers in Texas is biological control. The strategy involves using natural enemies that feed on arundo and could reduce its growth.In California and other parts of the US, there are no organisms that cause substantial feeding damage or mortality to arundo. The lack of natural herbivores has partly allowed the plant to flourish in areas it has invaded.Researchers searching for arundo's natural enemies in its native range have identified several insects that could potentially reduce the plant's vigour by feeding on it. These include the Arundo wasp, Tetramesa romana; the Arundo scale, Rhizaspidiotus donacis; and the Arundo fly, Cryptonevra species.Safety evaluations have found that these insects are highly host-specific and pose no substantial threat to other plants. Efforts are now under way to mass rear these natural enemies and establish them in areas with severe arundo infestations.In North America, arundo appears to reproduce mainly through asexual reproduction. Although the plant produces flowers, it seldom produces viable seeds. Instead, it mainly spreads through vegetative reproduction, either through underground rhizomes or plant fragments.That ability to spread, combined with its rapid growth and dense stands, has helped turn a plant introduced to California in the 1820s for roofing material and erosion control into a long-term invasive species problem.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Discussions focused on incorporating a special provision under Article 371 to protect the interests of the local population.He said the next meeting is scheduled for October, with the administration hoping to have an advanced draft of the proposed Constitutional Amendment Bill ready by then.What Ladakh is seekingThe proposed framework would include a Union Territory-level body elected directly through constituencies and vested with legislative and financial powers.The move comes amid demands for greater constitutional protection for Ladakh following its transition into a Union Territory.What does Article 371 provide?Articles 371 contain special provisions for specific states. These provisions differ from one state to another but broadly seek to protect local political, cultural, social and economic interests.Article 371-A, for instance, provides special safeguards for Nagaland. Articles 371-B and 371-C provide for special committees in the Legislative Assemblies of Assam and Manipur and similiarly other provisions are there for other states.If a new Article 371 provision is introduced specifically for Ladakh, it would be significant because Ladakh is a Union Territory rather than a state.The proposal would therefore require a constitutional arrangement tailored to a Union Territory, potentially making it different from the existing Article 371 provisions that primarily apply to states.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A year after his death, conservative students struggle to fill void left by Kirk
articles.summary: The assassination sent shockwaves through the conservative youth movement, which students say has lost momentum and a vital figurehead.
articles.body:
Jeb Jacobi still remembers the echo of the gunshot that killed Charlie Kirk.

He was a volunteer at the Turning Point USA event at Utah Valley University (UVU), where Kirk was set to engage in one of his famous live debates on 10 September last year.

But when the conservative activist collapsed, hit by a bullet fired from a sniper rifle, onlookers like Jacobi say they saw their hero become a martyr right before their eyes.

"It feels like there's a forever stain on us here," the third-year university student tells the BBC, as he reflects on the past year since Kirk's death. "This is where Charlie Kirk was killed."

In the wake of the assassination, Jacobi and many others thought that Turning Point USA (TPUSA), the organisation founded by Kirk, could only grow as Kirk's reputation as a conservative activist spread far and wide.

Now, he says, no-one has been able to fill the void.

"It's not the same organisation," he says. "It just doesn't have the same power, the same impact."

By contrast, one of TPUSA's chapter leaders elsewhere in the US denied any suggestion that the organisation was not what it was under Kirk - telling the BBC "this is quite literally just the beginning".

How a college dropout from the suburbs became Maga star Charlie Kirk

In the immediate aftermath of Kirk's death, support for TPUSA surged. A spokesperson posted on X five days after the killing that the organisation had received "over 32,000 inquiries in the last 48 hours to start new campus chapters".

Since then, however, many like Jacobi have noted a slowing momentum. There has been infighting between more moderate and right-wing factions within the organisation, current members say. In Arkansas, one chapter completely changed its name to disassociate itself from the Kirk-founded organisation, unhappy with the direction in which students felt it was heading.

The BBC contacted TPUSA for comment for this article, but has not received a response.

Utah Valley is located in a conservative area – where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats more than seven to one. But the shooting and political aftermath triggered a kind of culture war - on and off campus.

Jacobi feels his campus is more divided than ever now.

"The culture has gotten more hostile," he says.

"I love for everyone to have their own viewpoints and [be] sharing them," he adds. "The debate is good for society. It's what Charlie did."

Kirk made a name for himself by hosting debates on college campuses where he would spar with people who opposed his views. His popularity on campuses and online made him a rising star in the Republican Party, and President Donald Trump credited Kirk with helping getting young men to vote for him in the last election.

But critics argued that Kirk's debates were designed purely to stoke outrage and garner social media attention, while promoting misogyny, racism and homophobia.

Since his death, some students at UVU have protested against a campus memorial to the conservative activist. They have also tried to stop an event memorialising him from taking place on Thursday, the anniversary of Kirk's death.

Anthony Shinkle, another UVU student, notes how the school's TPUSA chapter and socialist clubs are often in conflict with each other on campus.

He fears Kirk's shooting, and its politically contentious aftermath, have made some supporters afraid to share their political ideology - and sent others further towards more extreme or fringe positions.

"These are impressionable people, impressionable youth," he said, noting how they watched their political hero "be murdered very, very graphically".

"I feel like the assassin got exactly what he wanted," Shinkle, who turns 21 next month, says. "It really feels like there's not anyone who can fill [Kirk's] shoes."

Earlier this month, a judge in Utah cleared the way for a trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of shooting Kirk. Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges.

Charlie Kirk murder suspect pleads not guilty as judge clears way for death penalty trial

Jacobi says many people have tried to fill the void left by the 31-year-old activist and father of two.

"Sure, they can echo the conservative message, but they can't do what Charlie did," he says. "He had such a way with his words to draw people in, to make them think, to debate, to get people involved."

"You just don't see that with anyone else," he adds. "I don't know if there will be another him."

Such a dip is not unusual following the assassination of a central founding figure like Kirk, says Mark Brewer, chair of the political science department at the University of Maine.

"You have a movement that was started and led by this kind of charismatic figure, and the charismatic figure goes away," he said. "A little bit of loss of momentum isn't exactly surprising."

He notes that Kirk's "personal status as a martyr remains very strong. You can see plenty of folks on the right who are trying to claim the… affiliation with Kirk."

"In some ways, that maybe has only increased," he said. "Kirk himself, in his own influence of his legacy, I don't think that's going anywhere."

Macy Gunnell, 22, started a TPUSA chapter at St Mary's College in Indiana following Kirk's death. She says she had tried for years to start one, but it was only after his death that she got the approval.

Gunnell acknowledges divisions within the organisation - but takes a more optimistic viewpoint.

"While there are flying accusations out there that Turning Point is dead, Turning Point's become something that it never was, Turning Point became everything Charlie hated - that could not be further from the truth," says Gunnell, 22, who has since graduated and works in media in Washington DC.

A debater still affiliated with TPUSA, Gunnell travelled to its headquarters over the summer and met Erika Kirk, the founder's widow who took over as CEO, along with the organisation's spokesman Andrew Kolvet.

"I'm confident that Turning Point's not going anywhere, and this is quite literally just the beginning," she says.

Gunnell is among the speakers featured in TPUSA's new Pick Up the Mic campaign - sending debaters to campuses and high schools across the country to continue Kirk's traditions engaging in the art of rhetoric. It begins this semester.

Back at UVU, Jacobi also hopes and believes TPUSA will still grow. He points to a fellow student who was never interested in politics but, after Kirk's death, now helps run their school's chapter of the group.

The killing of Kirk has shaken Shinkle, whose family in Alabama always told him how much safer Utah would be than his home state.

"I kind of feel a weird sense of guilt," he says. "I feel like it's a common sentiment, that everyone wishes they could have done something."

Jacobi, meanwhile, says he had turned to religion instead of deepening his connections with politics.

"When Charlie died, I took a look at myself," he says. "There are so many people who make politics their entire identity. It's so unhealthy for you."

"It really made me realise I needed and wanted a relationship with Christ like Charlie had," he adds. "Ever since I got more involved, I've felt much happier and more peaceful of a person."

And what happens to Turning Point, Prof Brewer says, remains to be seen.

"The final part of the story hasn't been written yet," he said. "So I think a lot will be determined over the next six, 12, 18 months."

articles.body: Rohit Rohit, 22, allegedly stalked and harassed a 38-year-old woman for months before fatally shooting her outside a Panera Bread restaurant in Sacramento on Tuesday, September 8, authorities said.The Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office said Rohit and the woman had known each other for about two years through work, although they were employed by different companies. Investigators believe Rohit developed a fixation on the woman, whose identity has not been released.How Rohit Rohit allegedly stalked the womanAuthorities said the woman found an Apple AirTag hidden under the hood of her vehicle in January, around the time investigators believe the stalking began. Investigators also said he obtained a copy of her apartment key and entered her home while she was sleeping.When confronted the next morning, Rohit reportedly claimed he had entered the apartment because he was worried something had happened to her after she failed to answer him.The woman initially declined to pursue criminal charges or seek a restraining order, but deputies remained in contact with her. In May, they again requested her to obtain a restraining order, which she eventually did.On July 29, the woman reported that Rohit had allegedly violated the order by leaving random grocery items at her front door, according to the sheriff’s office.Woman chased, shot outside PaneraOn September 8, Rohit allegedly parked near a shopping centre on Howe Avenue shortly before 3pm. articles.title: Denmark and Germany are turning an island into a giant offshore power hub; 3GW of wind energy will flow to two countries
articles.summary: Europe News: Denmark and Germany are developing Bornholm Energy Island as a major offshore wind hub in the Baltic Sea, designed to collect 3GW of electricity and s.
articles.body: Denmark and Germany are developing Bornholm Energy Island as a major offshore wind hub in the Baltic Sea, designed to collect 3GW of electricity and send it to both countries. The project will use the Danish island of Bornholm as a central point for the power generated by wind farms placed offshore. From there, electricity will travel through underwater and land-based cables to national grids in Denmark and Germany. The agreement marks a significant step towards sharing renewable energy across borders, while turning Bornholm into an important link in Europe’s expanding offshore power network.3GW Bornholm Energy Island will connect offshore wind to Denmark and GermanyThe Bornholm Energy Island project is centred on using the island as a power hub rather than simply building wind farms for Denmark alone. According to the European Commission, Denmark and Germany reached an agreement on the joint development of the project at the North Sea Summit in Hamburg on 26 January 2026. The Commission described it as the first key delivery of its Energy Highways initiative.The project is planned to link 3GW of offshore wind generation with the electricity grids of both countries. This means electricity produced in the Baltic Sea can become a shared resource rather than remaining tied to a single national system. The European Commission says the project could also provide a blueprint for similar offshore developments elsewhere in the European Union.How will the island handle electricity from the Baltic SeaThe Danish Energy Agency explains that the wind turbines will be installed around 15 kilometres from Bornholm’s coast. From the offshore wind farms, electricity will be brought to the island, where electrical equipment will prepare it for transmission over long distances.The power will then be sent through cables towards Zealand in Denmark and towards Germany. The Danish Energy Agency says the 3GW capacity could correspond to the electricity consumption of up to 4.5 million Danish and German households. It would also double Denmark’s existing offshore wind capacity, which the agency lists at 2.3GW. The arrangement is intended to make better use of electricity depending on where demand is highest.The project is designed as a shared European power systemThe island’s role goes beyond collecting electricity from nearby turbines. According to the Bornholm Energy Island (BEI) project website, wind farms will be connected through a single hub, allowing their electricity to reach consumers in Denmark and Germany while also providing capacity for cross-border electricity trading.The technical system will use 525kV high-voltage direct-current cables. Electricity from the wind farms will be concentrated at Bornholm before being carried through sea and land cables to substations in Zealand and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in Germany. The system will also allow Bornholm itself to remain connected to Zealand and continental Europe.That cross-border design is one of the project’s most significant features. Instead of each country developing separate offshore connections, the two countries are sharing infrastructure and the electricity produced through it.Why is Bornholm important to Denmark’s offshore wind plansFor Denmark, the project represents a substantial expansion of offshore wind generation. The Danish Energy Agency says that BEI was originally planned with a smaller capacity, but the target was increased from 2GW to 3GW in 2022.The project grew out of Denmark’s 2020 climate agreement and forms part of the country’s wider effort to expand renewable electricity. The agency says the energy island is expected to become one of the largest construction projects in Danish history.The island was selected not simply as a place to put electrical equipment, but as the central point where offshore generation can be gathered and then distributed in different directions. That makes the project particularly suited to cooperate with Germany.What infrastructure will connect the wind farms with GermanyThe power hub requires a large network of electrical equipment and cables on both sides of the border. Energinet and 50Hertz are jointly developing the project, with Energinet responsible for the Danish electrical infrastructure and 50Hertz involved in the German connection. The project website reports that 50Hertz’s planned connection will have a transmission capacity of 2,000MW, with much of the cable route running offshore.EU funding gives the cross-border project additional supportThe scale of Bornholm Energy Island has also attracted European backing. The European Commission says the project has been designated a Project of Common Interest and has received a €645 million grant through the Connecting Europe Facility.The funding is intended to support the infrastructure needed to connect offshore wind generation with the two national grids. The project website describes the planned connection as the world’s first hybrid direct-current interconnector of its kind.Bornholm is preparing for a major change in its landscapeThe energy project is also affecting the island itself. Electrical facilities are planned near Aakirkeby, while the surrounding area has undergone environmental and archaeological investigations.According to the BEI project website, archaeological pre-investigations near Aakirkeby have revealed evidence spanning thousands of years, including remains from the Stone Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age and Viking Age. More than 35 hectares have been identified for excavation, making the work the largest archaeological excavation planned on Bornholm.The project has also involved public consultation and environmental assessment. The website reports that Denmark granted an environmental permit covering the Danish onshore and offshore facilities and cables after consultation processes between 2022-25.Bornholm Energy Island is therefore becoming more than a wind-power project. It is being built as a shared electricity hub where offshore generation, national grids and cross-border energy trading meet. If completed as planned, its 3GW of wind power will give Denmark and Germany a common source of renewable electricity while offering a model for how future offshore energy hubs could connect several European countries.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Swinney asks prime minister for legal mechanism for independence vote
articles.summary: Scotland's first minister has written to Andy Burnham, asking for a meeting to discuss how another independence vote might be triggered.
articles.body:
First Minister John Swinney has written to the prime minister inviting him to meet and consider the constitutional future of Scotland.

Swinney's letter calls for a legal mechanism to be established for triggering an independence vote following comments from Andy Burnham which some have interpreted as a softening of his stance on the issue.

Burnham told MPs on Wednesday that both in Scotland and Northern Ireland, a border poll would be considered if public opinion had changed and there was a clear consensus.

But he added that he did not believe that had happened, and Downing Street later insisted there was no change in his position that such a vote was currently "off limits".

In his letter Swinney welcomed Burnham's remarks , claiming it signalled an acceptance that majority support for independence in Scotland should trigger a new referendum.

He said it was a "long-overdue acceptance of the reality that the people of Scotland will decide their own future".

He concluded: "Now that you have agreed the principle that Scotland should have a referendum when it is likely that people would vote for independence, it is important for us to meet to discuss how we turn that principle into an agreed legal mechanism, as exists in Northern Ireland."

Burnham was responding to a question at Prime Minister's Questions from Dundee SNP MP Chris Law.

Law noted that Burnham had said he would stick 100% to the terms of the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland and noted that the agreement includes a provision on what would trigger a referendum on leaving the UK.

He then asked whether the conditions for initiating a similar referendum in Scotland should also be set out in law.

Burnham replied that the Good Friday Agreement said a border poll "be considered by the Northern Ireland Secretary when there is clear consensus in the country—when public opinion has changed to the point at which the call has to be considered".

He continued: "I would say that it is exactly the same situation in Scotland. I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one."

A referendum on Scottish independence in September 2014 saw the country vote to remain part of the UK by a margin of 55% to 45%.

In July, in his first meeting with Swinney after becoming prime minister, Burnham said another such vote was "off limits" because it would take the focus away from priorities like growing the economy and helping families cope with the cost of living.

How much support is there for independence?

Sir John Curtice, professor of politics at Strathclyde University, said recent opinion polls suggested there is currently a very small majority in favour of independence.

But, given the small margins, any claim that this means Scotland is "likely" to vote to leave the UK is something that would be challenged, he told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast.

He said it was "probably possible to make a reasonable case" that the probability of a vote for independence is currently greater than zero, but that polling falls far short of suggesting it is "pretty damn certain".

He said there had previously been acknowledgement by some within the nationalist community that a referendum should be held when opinion polls consistently indicate about 60% in favour.

The SNP, when making the case for another referendum frequently cites the record number of pro-independence MSPs returned to Holyrood in the May election.

Between them the SNP and Scottish Greens ended up with 73 MSPs, increasing the pro-independence majority by one.

However, the proportion of the electorate voting for pro-independence parties fell significantly to about 41%, down from about 50% in 2021.

The mismatch between vote share and MSP total was explained by the pro-union vote becoming more fragmented, driven by the rise of Reform UK.

"The difficulty is that both sides in the argument can point to evidence to substantiate their case," said Curtice.

What have previous prime ministers said?

David Cameron was the prime minister who reached an agreement with then SNP leader Alex Salmond that a referendum could be held in 2014.

On the eve of the vote, he declared it was a "once and for all decision" and that there could be "no going back" and "no re-run".

He stuck to that view afterwards, saying the debate had been "settled for a generation"

Salmond had previously spoken of it being a "once in a lifetime, perhaps once in a lifetime opportunity" in his opinion, and had indicated that by "political generation" he meant something like the 18-year gap between previous constitutional referendums.

Salmond's successor as first minister, Nicola Sturgeon, later argued that the 2016 Brexit vote, where the UK as a whole voted to leave the EU while a majority of Scots voted to stay, represented a "material change of circumstances" which put another indyref vote back "on the table".

Cameron resigned after the Brexit vote, replaced by Theresa May , who repeatedly declared that "now is not the time" for another referendum.

One of her arguments was that it was too early because the Scottish people did not yet know what the outcome of leaving the EU would be.

When Boris Johnson entered Number 10 in 2019, he also rejected the call, harking back to the "once in a generation" description of the earlier vote.

During her brief tenure as prime minister in 2022, Liz Truss described Sturgeon as an "attention seeker" who she planned to ignore.

Rishi Sunak had taken over by the time the UK Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish government did not have the power to hold an independence referendum without the consent of the UK government.

And he argued that there were "more pressing issues" that the Scottish people wanted politicians to focus on.

After Labour came to power at Westminster in 2024, Sir Keir Starmer took a similar line, saying it was "not a priority" and he could not envisage one happening while he was prime minister.

What, if anything, has changed? The answer is both very little and a lot.

A lot because UK prime ministers tend to brush off calls for another independence referendum with a "now is not the time" sort of answer.

They usually stress that there are more important things to deal with at this point.

Andy Burnham has previously been more emphatic in telling John Swinney that the issue was "off limits".

Then in a brief exchange at prime minister's questions by drawing a parallel with Northern Ireland, he has appeared to open the door to further discussion about a formal agreement on the circumstances in which a further referendum could be considered.

I cannot remember any previous prime minister speaking in similar terms.

That's the difference but it changes very little in reality.

Andy Burnham is unlikely to agree to discussing a formal mechanism for another independence referendum in Scotland.

It was already clear that driving up support for such a course and the likelihood of a "yes" outcome is what the SNP and other independence supporters would need to achieve.

Andy Burnham has simply acknowledged that to be the case and inadvertently given nationalists a some encouragement in the process.

articles.title: How Charlie Kirk’s assassination changed the way conservatives approach hostile opponents
articles.summary: One year after Charlie Kirk's assassination, Turning Point USA allies weigh how to balance personal safety with showing up on college campuses.
articles.body: Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk built his public persona around confronting political opponents face-to-face, often in settings where disagreement and hostility were expected. Now, one year after his assassination, conservative media personalities and influencers are still wrestling with how to keep themselves safe while also sparking conversations with the other side. Some say Kirk's death has made them more cautious about security, while others feel more determined to keep showing up despite the danger. INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES For TPUSA reporter Savanah Hernandez, the answer is both, as she strives to cover important stories while also keeping herself safe. "I do feel myself, as a woman, I was awarded a little bit more ability to go and cover various events or talk to certain people without the threat of violence. But after Charlie's assassination, all of that changed," Hernandez told Fox News Digital. Hernandez recalled that during one of the first events she covered after Kirk's assassination, which was a protest outside a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility, someone realized she was with TPUSA and proceeded to "light a MAGA hat on fire" and put it in front of her face. Months later, in April 2026, Hernandez was physically assaulted while reporting outside an ICE facility in Minnesota. "As a journalist, I always want to get the story. I always want to get the shot. I always wanted to show my audience exactly what's going on, but, unfortunately, the reality of potentially dying on the street is something that I am very well aware of, as are all of my friends," Hernandez told Fox News Digital. Daily Wire co-founder and host of "The Ben Shapiro Show" Ben Shapiro told Fox News Digital that while he has had round-the-clock security for years, Kirk's assassination changed how he approaches certain events. "What I did say in the aftermath is I would never again do an outdoor event. Outdoor events are inherently riskier, very, very difficult to secure," Shapiro told Fox News Digital. Shapiro said that while his team takes precautions to secure events, such as requiring tickets and using metal detectors, he knows that "you can't bring the risk all the way down to zero." ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION Michael Knowles, host of "The Michael Knowles Show," warned of "two opposite errors" that some could make in the wake of Kirk's assassination. The first, he told Fox News Digital, is to "take security so seriously that you never do anything," thus handing your opponents a victory "because they've shut you up." The second, is to "not take security seriously at all, in which case the left can shut you up by killing you." "I think what Charlie endeavored to do and what we all endeavor to do is to have a prudent middle ground where we take the security seriously, but we don't allow the left to intimidate us into shutting up," Knowles told Fox News Digital. Knowles recalled that he was set to appear alongside Kirk at an event slated to take place at the University of Minnesota 12 days after the TPUSA founder's assassination. In fact, the last message he received from Kirk was about the event. "I remember thinking that morning, 'oh shoot, I owe Charlie a text, ah well, I'll get to it later,' and then he was killed," Knowles said. Shortly after Kirk’s assassination, Knowles said he was asked whether he still planned to attend the event in Minnesota. He told TPUSA that the decision was ultimately up to the organization, and organizers ultimately decided the event should proceed. "They said, ‘We think you should do it,’ which of course was the right answer," Knowles said. Knowles told Fox News Digital that he views the decision as being consistent with Kirk's values. He said that while he was reluctant to speak for the late TPUSA founder, he believed that Kirk would have wanted conservatives to continue to "show up, bring a message of conservatism, a message of Christianity and everything in between to college campuses. I'm quite certain he would say that's the right thing to do." Hernandez echoed a similar sentiment, saying that Kirk's assassination made her more determined to continue reporting from the ground. "Despite the uptick in violence and the increased threats that everybody at Turning Point USA has been experiencing after his assassination, I think we're more emboldened than ever to continue to stay on the ground because Charlie's entire thing was about having conversations with people to reach out to the other side," she said. Shapiro told Fox News Digital that, beyond security concerns, Kirk's assassination also underscored the broader problem with how political debates take place in the age of social media. "I think that the entire value of debate may have declined just as a facet of social media, because so much of debate is not really about free exchange of ideas anymore. Now it's much more about the 15-second dunk," Shapiro said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Shapiro added that social media-driven viral clips of debates have incentivized public figures to provoke opponents, rather than engage with them. "As the attention span decreases… you can score a point simply by getting up in front of a microphone and saying something egregious to somebody else," he said. Shapiro warned that increasingly heated rhetoric had led to what he called "permission structures for violence," which he said "have become commonplace in American public life." Knowles said he came to a sweeping conclusion following Kirk's assassination that differed from many in the conservative world. While some saw it as a moment to "double and triple down" on debating anyone, anywhere, Knowles said he drew the opposite lesson. "My lesson that I drew was that no one debated ideas in the open marketplace with anyone with greater graciousness and openness than Charlie Kirk. And they murdered him for it," Knowles told Fox News Digital, adding that "we need to properly regulate the marketplace." Still, many show up to voice their opinions, even when they face opposition.

articles.title: Ancient cult discovered in region traveled by Apostle Paul before Christianity took hold
articles.summary: Nine ancient inscriptions from Akmoneia in Phrygia, in modern-day Turkey, reveal the first proof of a Demeter fertility cult in the region tied to Apostle Paul's journeys.
articles.body: Millennia-old inscriptions uncovered in a region tied to the Apostle Paul are shedding new light on how ancient people practiced religion nearly 2,000 years ago. A recent study examined nine newly documented inscriptions discovered during a survey of Akmoneia, an ancient city in the historical region of Phrygia, in modern-day western Turkey. Hüseyin Uzunoğlu, an associate professor at Akdeniz University in Turkey, and Münteha Dinç, an associate professor at Uşak University, are the co-authors of the study, published in the journal Gephyra. ANCIENT BOOK OF REVELATION CITY GIVES UP STUNNING SECRET BURIED FOR 1,500 YEARS Phrygia is mentioned in the New Testament. It's associated with the missionary journeys of the Apostle Paul, who traveled through the region and helped spread Christianity across the Roman world. But the newly documented inscriptions — which date between the first and third centuries A.D. — highlight the religious traditions that already existed in the region. Among the most significant was an inscription concerning a statue of Demeter Karpophoros, a goddess associated with fertility and harvests. Uzunoğlu told Fox News Digital that while the cult was already well established elsewhere in Asia Minor, there had previously been no written proof of its presence in Phrygia. ARCHAEOLOGISTS IN ISRAEL UNCOVER 1,700-YEAR-OLD ROMAN-ERA STATUES BURIED FACE DOWN "But until this inscription — and a closely related one we published a couple of years ago — there was no epigraphic proof that the cult existed in Phrygia at all, even though Phrygia was a major agricultural region," he said. "So this fills in a real gap on the map of ancient religious practice." Another inscription revealed that a benefactor named Demades had commissioned a torch-bearing statue, likely helping to illuminate Akmoneia's colonnaded main street at night. "This wasn't just civic piety in the abstract. It was one wealthy citizen literally lighting up his city," Uzunoğlu said. "Torch-bearing statues are known from only two other sites … so it's a nice addition to a very short list." CONSTRUCTION WORKERS CLEARING OLD BOMBS UNEXPECTEDLY FIND 'IMPORTANT' ANCIENT SANCTUARY A different inscription honored a woman named Mandana as the city's high priestess. Her husband, Priscus, set up the monument. "We don't have all the details of Christian missions [in] that area, but we do know that there was a lot of dialogue and a lot of missionary work in the region." "There's good evidence … of women holding such positions independently," said Uzunoğlu. "Mandana's inscription looks like one of those cases: The honor is hers, not a shared one." RARE 1,200-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CROSS FOUND IN FIELD BY METAL DETECTORIST The inscriptions also offer glimpses into the personal lives of Akmoneia's inhabitants. Uzunoğlu said one funerary altar suggests that a tomb owner prepared the monument for himself and his wife on the condition that she remain unmarried after his death. Another funerary stone carries epitaphs for two men who were likely soldiers. The epitaph says that one of the men "fell victim to lawless hands," or was murdered, according to Uzunoğlu. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "They were probably comrades-in-arms commemorated together — a rare and human glimpse of military friendship in the epigraphic record," he said. Overall, Uzunoğlu said the importance of the research lies in what the inscriptions reveal together. "It's less about one blockbuster find than about how each new stone incrementally sharpens the picture of how Akmoneians worshipped, honored each other and buried their dead," said Uzunoğlu. While the inscriptions are not directly related to Christianity, they offer a window into the religious landscape of Phrygia, a region where the faith gained an early foothold, according to Douglas Estes, a scholar of early Christianity and professor at the New College of Florida. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Though Phrygia is associated with the missionary journeys of the Apostle Paul, Estes — who was not involved in the recently published research — cautioned that it is not known whether Paul traveled through Akmoneia itself. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "We don't have all the details of Christian missions [in] that area, but we do know that there was a lot of dialogue and a lot [of] missionary work in the region," he said. Estes said archaeological evidence points to Christianity gaining followers among ordinary people in Phrygia well before Emperor Constantine came to power. articles.title: Drug use may have begun 25,000 years ago, new research finds
articles.summary: Scientists have found evidence that early human foragers in Indonesia were using the betel nut as a drug.
articles.body:
Humans may have been using mind-altering substances far earlier than scientists had once thought, new research indicates.

The evidence shows that betel nuts were used as drugs by some Indonesian communities up to 25,000 years ago.

Scientists from Griffith University in Australia found unusual patterns in the skeletal remains of early human foragers, which they linked to the sucking of betel nuts.

Professor Adam Brumm, who led the research, said this may be the "earliest evidence for drug use anywhere in the world".

In the new study, published in Science Advances, the researchers reported the discovery of rare skeletal remains of two early human foragers from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. One dated to 25,000-16,000 years ago and the other to 7,600-6,300 years ago.

Both of the hunter-gatherers showed an unusual dental wear pattern with deep, rounded tooth grooves, which the researchers found was caused by sucking whole betel nuts.

When consumed, betel nuts – seeds of the betel or Areca catechu palm – induce a sense of mild euphoria and heightened awareness.

Brumm said: "Although poorly known in western societies, it is the world's fourth most widely used psychoactive substance, after alcohol, caffeine and nicotine."

It had previously been thought that drug-taking began after the advent of farming, beginning with fermented alcohol drinks about 13,000 years ago.

However, that theory "fails to account for the possibility that very ancient drug-taking lies at the roots of our most commonly used psychoactive substances", according to Brumm.

"By identifying the ancient practice underlying betel-nut chewing as we know it, the study implies that some modern drug-taking behaviours are deeply rooted in forager traditions."

In the modern era, the drug is taken by mixing a processed seed of the betel nut with slaked lime and other ingredients to form a "quid", which is chewed. The mixture is popular in South and South East Asia, and is chewed by about one-tenth of the globe's population.

Researchers conducted experiments where they soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva, and found that just sucking on intact betel nuts released enough of the psychoactive compounds to alter brain function.

The effects of sucking betel nuts may have been milder than modern quid chewing, but the team suggested that the habit was significant enough to cause severe gum disease.

articles.title: Amnesty: Russian recruitment of foreign nationals is human trafficking
articles.summary: Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals to fight in the war in Ukraine "amounts to human trafficking," Amnesty International said on Thursday. "Many recrui...
articles.body:
Amnesty International accuses Russia of human trafficking through recruitment of foreign nationals to fight in Ukraine.

Recruits were promised lucrative salaries, sign-up bonuses, and pathways to Russian citizenship, but many received nothing and were coerced into enlisting.

Amnesty interviewed foreign nationals from various countries who reported having their passports seized, inadequate military training, and contracts only in Russian.

Russia's recruitment of foreign nationals to fight in the war in Ukraine "amounts to human trafficking," Amnesty International said on Thursday.

"Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not fulfilled. While some received partial payments before being captured, many reported receiving nothing at all," the human rights organization said in a press release on the new report.

"Beyond financial remuneration, all those interviewed described promised pathways to Russian citizenship as a particular incentive."

Russian recruiters used coercion, fraud and deception to persuade foreigners to enlist in the Russian military, Amnesty said.

"The level of exploitation and coercion involved led us to conclude that in many cases this amounts to human trafficking, as defined under the UN's Palermo Protocol," said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International's secretary general.

Amnesty said it interviewed more than one dozen foreign nationals including from Colombia, Cuba, Egypt, Somalia and South Africa during six visits to two Ukrainian prisoner-of-war camps between 2024 and 2026.

Only three of those interviewed had knowingly signed a contract to fight in Ukraine, it said.

Prisoners of war from Brazil and Sri Lanka told Amnesty that, after signing the contracts, their passports and mobile phones were seized, according to the organization.

They also said that the contracts were in Russian only and that nobody spoke English. The recruits only received inadequate basic military training lasting around two weeks, according to the report.

Amnesty noted it was unable to conduct investigations in Russia where the organization has been banned since May 2025.

In Ukraine - no reports of human trafficking, but other problems

Amnesty said that it has received no evidence of possible human trafficking involving third-country nationals in the Ukrainian army.

However, there are indications of corruption, discrimination and mistreatment by superiors, it said, with the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry reportedly investigating the matter.

Just under 16,000 foreign nationals from more than 70 countries, including nearly 40% from Latin American countries, are currently serving in the Ukrainian army, which counts a total of some 880,000 troops, according to the latest information provided by Kiev.

According to Ukraine, more than 28,000 foreign nationals have enlisted in the Russian military since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The General Staff in Kiev recently put the total number of Russian troops at slightly above 720,000.

articles.title: Sri Lankan court overturns presidential pardon for hardline monk
articles.summary: Galagodaatte Gnanasara was sentenced in 2018 to six years for contempt of court and intimidating the wife of a missing cartoonist.
articles.body:
Sri Lanka's Supreme Court has overturned a presidential pardon granted to a hardline Buddhist monk and ordered him to serve the remainder of a six-year prison sentence for intimidating the wife of a missing political cartoonist.

Galagodaatte Gnanasara was sentenced in 2018 for contempt of court and intimidating Sanya Eknaligoda, the wife of Prageeth Eknaligoda who disappeared in 2010.

The monk had interrupted a court hearing to speak in support of military intelligence officials who were accused of abducting the cartoonist.

Gnanasara served less than a year of that sentence because he received a pardon from Maithripala Sirisena, who was the country's president at the time.

In his cartoons, Prageeth Eknaligoda depicted issues of media freedom, political power and social disadvantage.

His work was critical of the former president Mahinda Rajapaksa, a nationalist credited with the defeat of the Tamil separatist rebels in 2009 after a bloody civil war.

Eknaligoda went missing in 2010 and has not been seen since. His wife has led a campaign to trace his whereabouts, and accuses the authorities of not doing enough to investigate his disappearance.

Gnanasara, who leads the Bodu Bala Sena (BBS) or "Buddhist Power Force", was a supporter of Rajapaksa and his brother Gotobaya, who also later served as president.

In 2025, he received a separate nine-month prison term for insulting Islam and inciting religious hatred.

Sri Lanka rarely convicts Buddhist monks, and it is almost unheard of for one to receive a custodial sentence.

articles.title: A 15-year-old was missing after an 18-foot fishing skiff failed to return near Alaska; rescuers found him clinging to the capsized vessel about 4 miles offshore
articles.summary: US News: A 15-year-old boy was rescued after he was found clinging to an overturned fishing boat about four miles east of St. Lawrence Island in Alaska. The Co.
articles.body: A 15-year-old boy was rescued after he was found clinging to an overturned fishing boat about four miles east of St. Lawrence Island in Alaska. The Coast Guard located him on Monday afternoon after three boaters had been reported missing. Two other people were found dead in the water.According to USGS, the three had been reported missing after their 18-foot fishing boat failed to return as expected. Alaska State Troopers notified authorities about the missing boaters at about 8.30 pm on Sunday after the vessel was confirmed to be overdue. The boat had last been seen on Friday after leaving the area of Savoonga on St. Lawrence Island.The boat was expected to return to St. Lawrence Island at about 3 am on Sunday. However, it did not return, leading to a search operation. Weather conditions and poor visibility prevented Coast Guard crews from beginning their search until Monday morning.The search eventually led rescuers to the capsized vessel, where the teenager was still holding on. At about 3 pm, a Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules aircraft from Air Station Kodiak spotted the survivor. The aircraft crew dropped a raft and survival equipment to help with the rescue.Teen found suffering from hypothermiaThe 15-year-old was experiencing symptoms of hypothermia when he was rescued from the overturned skiff. Hypothermia occurs when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, causing body temperature to fall to dangerously low levels.After locating the teenager, Coast Guard watchstanders at the Arctic District command centre coordinated his rescue with the Northwest Explorer, a nearby good Samaritan vessel. The aircraft crew had to leave the area to refuel, but before doing so, they deployed a line of flares to help guide the vessel towards the overturned boat.The Northwest Explorer reached the capsized skiff and took the teenager aboard. The same vessel also recovered the two other boaters, who were found unresponsive in the water. The survivor and the remains of the two deceased boaters were later transported to Nome, a city in western Alaska.Officials did not identify the three boaters. CBS News reported that the two people who died were the teenager's brother and cousin, citing the Anchorage Daily News. The teenager reportedly told the captain of the Northwest Explorer that he had remained clinging to the capsized boat for several days.“That is one remarkably tough kid, is all I can say,” captain Adam White told the Anchorage Daily News.Multiple aircraft joined the searchThe rescue operation involved several agencies and aircraft. The Coast Guard Arctic District coordinated the search with the Alaska Rescue Coordination Center, the Alaska Air National Guard's 176th Wing units, the 211th Rescue Squadron and 212th Rescue Squadron from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska State Troopers and local authorities in Savoonga.Two HC-130 aircraft and two MH-60 Jayhawk helicopters from Coast Guard Air Station Kodiak were launched during the operation. A 211th Rescue Squadron HC-130 with 212th Rescue Squadron Guardian Angels also assisted in the search.Rear Adm. Bob Little, commander of the Coast Guard's Arctic District, expressed condolences to the families and communities affected by the deaths.“Our hearts go out to the families, friends, and communities affected by the tragic loss of these two mariners," Little said. “We are grateful for the incredible efforts of the motor vessel Northwest Explorer, Federal, State, Village first responders and mission partners who assisted in the effort that resulted in a life saved.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
